Title: ‘Staggering’: watchdog condemns police after Indigenous teenager on bus wrongfully arrested – then searched

The commonwealth and ACT ombudsman has criticised the Australian federal police for failing to clearly define “racial profiling” after police in Canberra pulled guns on an Indigenous teenager they mistook for a suspect in an aggravated burglary.
The scathing investigation, released on Tuesday, made eight recommendations to the Australian federal police (AFP) and ACT policing after investigating the November 2025 incident. ACT policing sits under the AFP as the community policing arm.
The 17-year-old boy, referred to by the pseudonym Jay in the ombudsman’s report, boarded a bus in Woden on the evening of 11 November 2025.
ACT police stopped the bus and three officers entered with guns drawn. After being taken off the bus at gunpoint, Jay was then brought to the ground, handcuffed and arrested, the report said.
Less than 90 seconds later, police realised their mistake. Police had mistaken him for a suspect in an aggravated burglary.
Police released Jay, apologised to him and searched him. He then got back on the bus to continue his journey. Police did not ask for his name, confirm his age, or ask for details to contact a family member, according to the ombudsman’s report.
Iain Anderson, the commonwealth and ACT ombudsman, concluded that Jay was searched “inappropriately and seemingly unlawfully” after he was released from arrest.
“One of the other police who was there said, ‘Hey, here’s an opportunity. Let’s search him anyway even though we know he’s not the person we’re looking for,’” Anderson said.
“It was a bit staggering for me to see that that was their approach.”
The ombudsman found no evidence that Jay’s Aboriginality led to increased use of force. But Anderson said he was concerned that the AFP “had no clearly understood definition of ‘racial profiling’”.
The teenager’s family welcomed the “comprehensive and detailed report” from the ombudsman, saying it showed serious systemic failures within the AFP.
The 17-year-old’s family said he was travelling to his aunty’s house and was “compliant and polite during the entire incident”.
“The failures are numerous and deeply concerning,” the family said in a statement issued via lawyer Sam Tierney.
“They include a complete failure to provide any care … after subjecting him to a traumatic incident despite knowing he was a child, making public statements after the incident which inappropriately attempted to downplay and diminish the incident and an apparent failure of the AFP internally to understand what racial profiling is.”
The description of the alleged offender for the burglary included the term “Aboriginal male”.
Anderson said the use of “Aboriginal” as a physical descriptor was unhelpful and relied on the use of an “outdated, stereotypical physical trait”.
He acknowledged ACT policing were responding to a fast-evolving incident but concluded there were opportunities to improve the force’s engagement with First Nations communities and their aftercare of “innocent people who are caught up in their actions”.
“Altogether, the incident lasted just under four minutes. But it, and its aftermath, have had serious repercussions for Jay and his family and on the already fragile relationship between ACT policing and the ACT’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities,” the report said.
The report’s recommendations include that ACT policing review its use of race as a proxy to describe a person’s physical traits, adopt objective descriptors and develop clearer guidance to support officers performing the role of “Alpha 8” to make decisions on command of an incident. Alpha 8 is a role assigned to an on-duty inspector with responsibility for the strategic overview of policing resources.
The recommendations have been accepted.
The AFP accepted in principle the recommendation that it establish a clearly understood definition of “racial profiling” aligned with the objectives of Australia’s Racial Discrimination Act. The ombudsman said the definition should be included in the AFP’s order on professional standards, which establishes internal guidance.
The AFP said these orders were not the appropriate place to embed racial profiling. It said it would undertake a review of AFP and ACT policing governance to determine if additional clarification would support members in applying the relevant principles.
An internal investigation by the AFP’s professional standards unit found Jay’s search breached their code of conduct but concluded discrimination did not lead to the mistaken arrest.
“The AFP can confirm that there was no evidence to suggest race or other discriminatory factors influenced interactions between police and the young person, or that excessive force was used during the arrest,” an AFP statement published on Tuesday morning said.
In correspondence to the ombudsman, Krissy Barrett, the AFP commissioner, said it was “committed to continuous improvement and to rebuilding trust and strengthening relations between the community and its police force”.
Last year, the ACT’s chief police officer, Scott Lee, apologised for the incident and acknowledged the trauma it would have caused Jay, his family and the broader Indigenous community.
Lee told the ombudsman he remained committed to building and strengthening its relationship with the ACT’s First Nations community.

Title: Saman Bird Sanctuary to get tourism boost as UP Cabinet approves land transfer

Saman Bird Sanctuary to get tourism boost as UP Cabinet approves land transfer
Lucknow, The Uttar Pradesh Cabinet on Tuesday approved the free transfer of six hectares of Gram Sabha land near Saman Bird Sanctuary in Mainpuri to the Tourism Department for developing tourist facilities and promoting birdwatching and nature tourism.
The site will be known as Mayank Rishi Bird Sanctuary.
The decision will pave the way for connecting the area with tourism facilities and attracting tourists from India and abroad, the UP government said in a statement.
The decision was taken at a Cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Tuesday.
Saman Bird Sanctuary in Mainpuri is an important wetland and Ramsar Site in Uttar Pradesh. It is a major habitat for large numbers of migratory birds.
Located in the Gangetic plains, this seasonal lake has become an attraction for birdwatchers, nature lovers and photography enthusiasts.
Finance Minister Suresh Khanna said that during the migratory season, numerous species of birds arrive at Saman Bird Sanctuary from different parts of the country as well as from abroad.
Uttar Pradesh is home to several important bird sanctuaries, including Chandrashekhar Azad Bird Sanctuary, Sandi Bird Sanctuary in Hardoi, Bakhira Bird Sanctuary in Sant Kabir Nagar, Vijay Sagar Bird Sanctuary in Mahoba, Lakh Bahosi Bird Sanctuary in Hamirpur and Samaspur Bird Sanctuary in Agra.
Large numbers of migratory birds, particularly during autumn, arrive at these sites. The natural beauty and biodiversity of Saman Bird Sanctuary make it an ideal destination for birdwatching, photography and nature tourism. There is also potential for visitors to observe birds from boats at close range and through watchtowers.
The UP government is focusing on developing bird sanctuaries by incorporating them into national and international birdwatching circuits, developing basic infrastructure, and creating facilities such as watchtowers, signboards, solar lighting and biodiversity study centres.
At the same time, action plans are being prepared for the conservation of migratory birds and the convenience of tourists.
The transfer of 6 hectares of land near Saman Bird Sanctuary to the Tourism Department will further enhance the possibilities of expanding tourist facilities in the area, the statement said.

Title: Lloyds Bank is holding on to our urgently needed £5,500

Last November, Lloyds Bank informed me, in my role as treasurer of my parish church, that the church account was to be closed and that I should open a new business account instead. This can only be done online, but a fault with their system prevented me – and local branch staff – from doing so.
At the branch staff’s suggestion, I opened the new account with a different bank in early March. Since then, I’ve been trying in vain to get Lloyds to transfer the balance from the closed account.
I’ve been repeatedly told to visit my local branch and repeatedly told that the money would arrive within weeks. At one point I was told that the bank had lost my identity verification documents and so had put the case at the bottom of the pile.
We are owed nearly £5,500, which, for a congregation of 10 in a village of 60 houses, is a significant sum. We have had to borrow from parishioners to pay for essential repairs and to settle the electricity bill.
CI, Yorkshire
The apparent indifference of Lloyds is outrageous. As was its energy spurt when it realised public exposure was pending.
As soon as I questioned its inertia, it winged off a mea culpa acknowledging poor and inconsistent communications and offering £400 in goodwill, plus £96 in lost interest.
What the letter from the executive complaints manager did not mention was the still-missing funds.
So back I had to go to Lloyds, and off went another letter from the bank apologising for the omission.
The money was transferred more than four months after the account was closed.
A Lloyds spokesperson said: “We’re sorry the customer had such a difficult experience. We should have handled things better.”

Title: Harvesting rice and crabs on one field offers farmers a climate-resilient alternative

- In Assam, women are cultivating indigenous rice varieties like Betguti and integrating freshwater crab farming to cope with erratic rainfall and prolonged dry spells, offering a climate-resilient alternative to traditional paddy cultivation.
- Crabs help control pests, aerate the soil and reduce the need for agrochemicals, while providing the farmers with a second source of income.
- Supported by the Assam State Rural Livelihood Mission, this women-led integrated farming method is being scaled across 219 blocks in the state.
The harsh summer sun was beating down their backs, yet farmers in Assam’s Borborua block in Dibrugarh district went about their paddy cultivation. Waddling through paddy fields submerged in the rainwater of the past few weeks, they hummed songs and chatted as they planted Betguti (Oryza sativa), an indigenous variety of rice that holds the promise of withstanding the increasingly unpredictable weather — erratic rainfall and long dry spells.
Once the planting is done, they will release freshwater crabs in the field. Alongside the rice, the crabs will grow too, sustaining each other and offering the women a way to sustain their families amid rising concerns of climatic change and land degradation .
This women-led integrated rice-crab farming method is emerging as a climate-resilient alternative to traditional paddy cultivation in Assam.
Climatic changes challenge traditional ways
Traditionally, paddy-fish farming has been practiced in pockets of Assam, particularly areas that are vulnerable to floods. In this type of farming, fish spawns are either introduced in the flooded fields where the indigenous Bau-dhaan rice variety is grown, or enter the fields during monsoon from adjacent water bodies and grow along with paddy. “This integrated farming practice in which fish is grown as a ‘second crop’, however, has become challenging because of the long dry spells that Assam has been witnessing,” said Samir Bordoloi, a farmer and advocate of natural farming techniques. “Now, we have heavy spells of rain, and then long dry spells,” he said. “Rearing fish during these dry spells is not easy.”
Erratic weather patterns have also had an impact on agriculture as a whole, including paddy cultivation. In such a context, hybrid rice varieties promise better productivity, he says. According to the Economic Survey of Assam 2025-2026, hybrid rice cultivation area (as a share of total rice cultivation area) in the state has grown from almost 8% in 2018-19 to nearly 13% in 2024-25. High-yielding varieties of rice span 74%.
“But even those hybrid varieties cannot tolerate long dry spells,” Bordoloi said. The indigenous Betguti, on the other hand, is climate resilient, can withstand long dry periods and can be planted until late July — at least a month after the usual planting cycle. It is ready to be harvested in 150 days.
Giving indigenous rice a chance
In 2025, a conversation between Bordoloi and officials of the Assam State Rural Livelihood Mission (ASRLM) on promoting organic farming, steered towards indigenous varieties of rice. ASRLM leads a women-led organic and natural farming programme across 219 blocks in the state. It was an opportunity, according to Bordoloi, to use this platform to encourage the cultivation of indigenous varieties of rice. “Instead of monoculture, we spoke about integrated farming, like fish-paddy farming, through which farmers can have more than one source of income,” he said. “But instead of fish, our local variety of mud crabs seemed more viable because of climatic changes.”
With the support of ASRLM, the Narayanpur block of Lakhimpur district was chosen for this project that started the same year. The indigenous Betguti seeds were procured from Kusherswar Kochari, a farmer in a different district.
Nikumoni Bora, a farmer, stepped forward to try this crab-paddy farming on one bigha (0.33 acres) of her farmland. For Nikumoni, the primary motivation was personal. She wanted to save indigenous varieties of rice from disappearing.
“In my block, we mostly grow indigenous varieties of rice,” she said. “But hybrid rice is also being grown in patches. It is becoming difficult to predict the weather; so as a farmer myself, I understand the need to diversify,” she said. The aim, therefore, is not to make “hybrid rice disappear” but to “save indigenous rice from being lost”.
Along with Nikumoni, 79 other women — Krishi Sakhis, or Community Agriculture Care Service Providers under ASRLM — stepped in to plant Betguti. After the saplings took root, they released crabs in the field too.
How crabs supported rice cultivation
In the paddy fields, the crabs played an important role. “They ate the pests of the crop,” Nikumoni said, “And as they grew, I realised that the soil in the field became soft because the crabs were aerating it, which helped the rice plants grow better.”
Her observation is backed by research. Studies on rice-crab farming have shown improvement in soil nutrient levels, rice productivity and nutrient uptake, soil fertility, soil carbon and C:N ratio, biodiversity, water purification, and effective utilisation of available resources in the form of land and water.
Other research has found that aquatic animals in rice paddies reduce weeds, increase yield, and help maintain stable soil nitrogen. Pallab Kumar Sarma, chief scientist, All India Coordinated Research Project for Dryland Agriculture (AICRPDA), at the Biswanath College of Agriculture, finds this form of integrated farming promising, “to increase farmers’ income and ensure nutritional security. It is also sustainable, because it reduces the use of agrochemicals and pesticides,” Sarma added.
Nikumoni harvested nearly two quintals of rice from the 8 kilogram seeds that she planted on her land. The crabs, meanwhile, grew four times in three months, and she sold them in the local market at ₹300-400 per kilogram. Some of the harvest was also saved for consumption at home. She also sold seeds of the indigenous rice variety. In the past year, she earned ₹1.35 lakh (₹135,000), which supplements her family income and the honorarium she receives as a Krishi Sakhi.
More women taking up rice-crab farming
Enthused by her success, other women in the locality have now come forward to try their hand in rice-crab farming, too. Anjali Bora in Lakhimpur is one of them. “I have never planted rice before, but when I came to know about Nikumoni Baidew’s efforts, I wanted to try rice-crab farming too,” she said.
Anjali, Nikumoni and 58 other women of the locality who are part of a women-led farmers producer group have now leased a 20-bigha (about six acres) land to plant indigenous varieties of rice. “We will also release crabs in portions of this land; not all of it, because it will be difficult for us to harvest such large numbers,” Anjali said.
Nikumoni has also sent 60 kg seed of her harvested Betguti rice to the nearby Dibrugarh district where, under ASRLM, similar efforts of rice-crab farming are now being undertaken by farmers.
Anirban Roy of ASRLM said that they plan to promote this integrated, natural farming in 219 blocks of Assam. “We invited almost 260 women farmers from 80 blocks to come for a training this time in Dibrugarh,” Roy said, “Along with Betguti, 25 other indigenous varieties of rice have also been planted in 12 bighas (about four acres) of land.”
ASRLM will now draw up a nutritional chart for indigenous rice varieties like Betguti to make people aware about its health benefits, Roy said. “We can promote indigenous rice through the National Health Mission, and introduce it in mid-day meals in school.”
Since the market demand for indigenous rice exists, the women hope their efforts will bear fruit. “Us women, we don’t give up easily, especially if we know that something is good for our families and for our environment,” Nikumoni said. “As a mother myself, I want my children to eat healthy. These natural farming methods also require little investment and give good returns. So we will take this forward.”
As climate change continues to reshape Assam’s agricultural landscape, farmers like Nikumoni and Anjali are constantly experimenting and rewriting the rules of cultivation.

Title: NEET-UG protests case: Petitioners seek re-constitution of high-powered enquiry committee

Petitioners urgently sought before Chief Justice of India Surya Kant a re-constitution of the “under-equipped” high-powered enquiry committee (HPEC) chaired by former apex court Judge R. Subhash Reddy constituted to probe all issues concerning the police crackdown on students protesting NEET-UG paper leaks on July 20.
An application filed by the petitioners clarified that they were not commenting on the personal integrity of any members of the HPEC, but they said the “enquiry is required to test the role of persons occupying the highest levels of the Union Executive, the Ministry of Home Affairs, Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force”.
Editorial | Force of law: On the Delhi police
“This investigation would require enquiry into the role played by Union Home Minister, Mr. Amit Shah; officials within the Ministry of Home Affairs; Commissioner of Police Delhi, Mr. Anurag Kumar; Special Commissioner(s) of Police and Joint Commissioner(s) of Police, Delhi Police; Inspector General, Rapid Action Force, Seema Dhundia; other high-ranking officials from Rapid Action Force. This investigation would require enquiry into the specific role played by each of the individuals and officers,” the application, mentioned by senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, advocates Prashant Bhushan, Neha Rathi, Subhash Chandran, contended.
The application said the span of the enquiry would cover the specific directions passed by them or on before July 20; directions passed by them to ensure that order is maintained at the protest site; directions passed by them to ensure that use of force was proportional; directions to personnel of Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force not to wear uniform or name tags; disciplinary action taken against personnel deployed for the indiscriminate and excessive use of force, for not wearing uniforms and/or name tags, for using banned arms and equipment, and for outraging modesty of women.
“When the allegations require scrutiny of such high-ranking officials, the enquiry must be visibly and decisively insulated from executive and institutional influence and any perceived bias,” the application said.
Also Read | Protest venue under a web of cameras and facial recognition systems
Chief Justice Surya Kant tried to assuage apprehensions, saying the HPEC would be functioning under the eye of the Supreme Court itself.
The application however pointed out that publicly available information about the non-judicial members of the HPEC did not disclose specialised experience in independently investigating allegations of excessive police force or examining the conduct of senior serving executive and police officials.
Besides Justice Reddy, the committee includes Justice Ravi Shankar Jha, former Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court; Justice Shalinder Kaur, former Judge of the Delhi High Court; Rishi Kumar Shukla, former Director of the Central Bureau of Investigation; and Dr. L.R. Bishnoi, retired Director General of Police, Meghalaya.
The petitioners said information available in the public domain show a “long association between members and the executive authorities of the Union of India, including the Union Home Minister, highlighting that there is a reasonable apprehension of institutional deference which may prejudice the independent and impartial probe”.
Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the government, said the fears expressed by the petitioners were completely unwarranted and without basis. He strongly objected to naming individuals, and said the petitioners were trying to impose their will on the court. Mr. Sankaranarayanan said the petitioners were not doing anything of the sort, and was merely seeking an early listing of the application.
The petitioners argued that there was a “real risk that the enquiry may remain confined to acts of field-level personnel and fail to examine the decisions and omissions of senior authorities”.
The application said the HPEC, constituted in an apex court order on August 18, did not include any of the suggestions made by the petitioners, including that it should be headed by a former Chief Justice of India, have a retired woman DGP and a former Attorney General in its ranks.
The petitioners said the HPEC did not have officers with investigative skills or individuals with an established track record of civil liberties and public interest. They said their concerns were limited to the structure of the HPEC, which in its current form did not possess the “demonstrable independence and proficiency necessary for the enquiry to be carried out.
“To ensure that the probe is holistic, it is necessary that the HPEC must possess, collectively, demonstrated expertise in constitutional and civil rights, criminal investigation, forensic appreciation, crowd-control and use-of-force protocols, and enquiry into the role of senior functionaries without fear or favour,” the application said.

Title: Invasives impact in Global South needs more attention

Global biodiversity assessments have often suggested that the impacts of invasive alien species are greatest in wealthy countries of the Global North. A new study, however, challenges this notion and establishes that the severity of environmental impacts is generally higher in the Global South and calls out research bias for distorting the global picture.
The study, published recently in Science journal, combines two global datasets: GIDIAS, which contains more than 22,000 documented impacts involving over 3,300 invasive alien species from more than 6,700 scientific and grey-literature sources across 172 countries, and SInAS, which records the distribution of more than 39,700 alien species worldwide.
Considering research effort and the number of reports are much higher in the Global North, simply counting invasive species or documented impacts can make the region appear disproportionately affected. To better understand the impact, researchers, Sven Bacher, Petr Pyšek and Hanno Seebens used the IUCN’s Environmental Impact Classification for Alien Taxa (EICAT) under which an impact is considered severe when an invasive species causes a decline in a native population, local extirpation or global extinction.
Rather than simply counting how many invasive species or impacts have been recorded in a region, the researchers calculated average impact severity: the proportion of documented impacts that are severe. This was intended to reduce the effect of differences in research effort between countries.
The key findings include higher average impact severity in the Global South, the influence of research bias on assessments of invasive species impacts, the particular vulnerability of emerging economies, and the role of governance and management capacity in determining impact severity than large economies in the Global North.
The paper identifies India as one of the large, high-income developing economies where this pattern is visible. India has relatively high absolute numbers of documented impacts, but also a distinctly higher average impact severity than large economies in the Global North.
One of the biggest takeaways from the study is that weak governance and limited management capacity act as major drivers of high impact severity. Failure to recognise the Global South as facing the highest IAS impacts diverts attention away from the most threatened regions.
Previous research has identified emerging economies as countries likely to see the largest increases in alien species numbers in the near future as a result of strong economic development, potentially leading to more impacts, many of them severe. By contrast, wealthy countries of the Global North may have high introduction rates of alien species but also stronger governance and better management capacity as compared with the Global South, allowing them to implement policies and manage invasive species more effectively. The paper shows that good governance and effective management can reduce the impacts of biological invasions across most taxa and ecosystems.

Title: Several injured as police stop Bihar students’ protest march

A protest by students in Patna turned violent on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) when police used batons and water cannons to stop them from marching to the Bihar Chief Minister’s residence.
Protesting in Patna since August 18, the students have made various demands, including changes to the format of the Teacher Recruitment Examination (TRE), which is currently held in two rounds - preliminary and main. The students are demanding that the test be held in a single phase without negative marks. Other demands include transparency in all competitive examinations, end to alleged discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in exams held by the Bihar Public Service Commission (BPSC), and a high-level independent inquiry into previous exam controversies.
ALSO WATCH Bihar student protest: Police use water cannons as BPSC aspirants march towards CM’s residence
On Tuesday (August 25, 2026), hundreds of students gathered at J.P. Golambar near Gandhi Maidan to start the march toward Lok Sevak Awas, the official residence of the Chief Minister. The protesters, backed by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), All India Students’ Association (AISA) and other student organisations, broke through the police barricades at Dak Bungalow Chowk at the heart of the city, leading to clashes with the police.
Several students as well as police personnel were injured in the scuffle, including a Deputy Superintendent of Police who suffered severe injuries in the stone-pelting by the protesters. A few girl students fainted. Due to the protest and the road blockade, vehicular movement was severely affected, leaving motorists stuck for hours. Many protesters were also detained by the police.
The escalation of the protests also came in the wake of controversial remarks made by BPSC Examination Controller Rajesh Kumar Singh on Monday (August 24, 2026) while addressing a press conference in Patna. To a question regarding the protests by students, Mr. Singh had quoted the Hindi proverb “Hathi chale bazaar, kutta bhaunke hazar” (focused people should ignore irrelevant criticisms). Mr. Singh had since expressed regret, saying he had no intention to hurt anyone’s feelings and that he was quoted out of context.
On Monday (August 23, 2026), Leader of Opposition Tejashwi Yadav met the protesting students at the venue and urged the government not to ignore voices of the protesting youth but to establish a positive dialogue with them.
“I demand that immediate and necessary steps be taken in this matter, prioritising the future of lakhs of students and youth in Bihar; otherwise, the united strength of the students and youth will compel the government to do so,” Mr. Yadav had said.
To resolve the problems of students, Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary had launched the ‘Vidyarthi Sahyog’ portal to convey students’ issues and suggestions directly to the government. Student support camps will also be organised to address students’ grievances on the fourth Tuesday of every month, the government said.
On August 18, the Bihar government issued the notification for 32,388 teaching posts to be filled by the TRE.
The students in the State are also demanding that fair decisions be taken regarding filling up vacant posts for Assistant Professor, relaxation in age limits and 100% domicile-based recruitment in government jobs and teacher appointment, and job security for guest Assistant Professors. They are also pressing for dates for all pending examinations and the issuance of an annual examination calendar covering all exams be made mandatory.

Fertilisers and Chemicals Travancore (FACT) shares sharply rallied 13% to cross Rs 887 apiece on Tuesday morning, while Rashtriya Chemicals and Fertilisers (RCF) shares surged around 8%. Paradeep Phosphates shares rallied over 7%, while Chambal Fertilisers & Chemicals shares gained around 4%.
Russia assures India of uninterrupted supply of fertilisers
Russia on Monday assured India of uninterrupted supply of energy and fertilisers amid disruption caused by the Middle East conflict, as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar met President Vladimir Putin. "We are doing everything we can to fully meet the needs of Indian farmers and the agricultural sector, increasing these supplies and standing ready to continue doing so," Putin was quoted as saying by the state-run TASS news agency during his meeting with Jaishankar.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi looks forward to meeting you at the SCO summit, then welcoming you in India for the BRICS Summit, and in due course, as per your mutual convenience, having the annual summit…So, we have, Excellency, I think a very strong picture of cooperation,” Jaishankar said.
The Russian President highlighted that Jaishankar's visit underscored the level of relations Russia and India had built over decades. He said cooperation was underway in virtually all areas, including at the level of the two governments, parliaments and businesses, according to TASS.

The elevated global prices of finished products and LNG have led to the government using up around 56% of the annual fertiliser subsidy in less than five months into the new financial year 2026-27, the Times of India reported.

Production of these complex fertilisers fell 28% YoY to 19.2 lakh tonnes from 26.64 lakh tonnes a year earlier, while imports slipped 48.5% to 4.9 lakh tonnes from 9.54 lakh tonnes, said industry officials, citing data from the Fertiliser Association of India (FAI).

Title: The kids are showing India a new kind of politics

Something remarkable is happening in India. The generation that was expected merely to sit in classrooms, memorise textbooks, and prepare for examinations is beginning to ask a fundamental question: What kind of school are we being asked to study in?
The Gen Z agitation at Jantar Mantar had already broken an important psychological barrier. A people terrorised into silence saw their government being tamed. For weeks, the youth peacefully agitated over examination irregularities and demanded the resignation of the Education Minister, making him accountable. They faced police barricades, threats of eviction, and endured a hunger strike. Then, on their way to Parliament, they had to brave the brutality of the police—lathi charge, tear gas shells, and pellet guns—but they forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign on July 25. The victory was symbolic but important; its larger significance lay elsewhere: it kindled a hope of change, dispelled fear of the government, and rejuvenated confidence that the people can win.
That discovery appears to have travelled downward—and outward. On August 15, as Narendra Modi delivered his Independence Day address from the Red Fort, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) launched a new campaign, “School Thik Karo” (Fix the Schools) a social audit of government school deficiencies.
The campaign has already encountered resistance, which reveals its political significance. In Bankura, West Bengal, 25-year-old CJP volunteer Shaik Abdul Hafeez visited Karisunda West Para Primary School on August 13 as part of School Thik Karo and filmed its dilapidated condition. According to his family, Hafeez and his father, Sheikh Mohammad Mafik, were subsequently assaulted by a mob reportedly belonging to the BJP. Mafik suffered severe head injuries and died two days later. Police have arrested eight people, while allegations of political involvement remain under investigation. Hafeez refused government compensation and instead demanded that a world-class school be built in his father’s name. The episode gives the campaign a grim new meaning: a demand for a functioning school has become a demand that power become answerable.
Meanwhile, schoolchildren have begun organising themselves, without any coordination from the top. So far, agitations have taken place in Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, and Bihar. They are rapidly multiplying, and they demand teachers, classrooms, toilets, drinking water, electricity/fans, school buildings, roads to schools, mid-day meals, protection against school closure/merger, and basic dignity of the learning environment. The authorities are nonplussed and unsure how to handle them. There is no central command, manifesto, or ideological programme behind any of this. That is precisely what makes it interesting.
Gen Alpha is showing Gen Z—and the rest of us—what politics can look like when it begins with an issue rather than an ideology.
Scale of the wound
To understand why this could spread rather than fade, look at the field of grievance available to them. Government data for 2024-25 records roughly 24.69 crore students across 14.72 lakh schools, taught by just over 1 crore teachers—government schools make up 69 per cent of that system and educate half the country’s children. This is not a marginal sector. It is one of the largest social institutions on earth.
And it is failing on its own terms. Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 found that only 44.8 per cent of Class V children in government schools could read a Class II text, and barely a quarter could do simple division sums. A child can sit through five years of government schooling in India and still not read fluently at the level expected of an eight-year-old. This describes what the state has actually delivered to tens of millions of families.
The dropout data tells the same story from a different angle. Even after recent official improvement, roughly 42.7 lakh children dropped out at the secondary stage alone in 2024-25. Secondary school retention nationally is just 47.2 per cent—that is, fewer than half the children who enter school complete schooling. In West Bengal, the secondary school dropout rate touches 20 per cent; in several States and Union Territories it is above 15 per cent. A parliamentary standing committee flagged 30-50 per cent teacher vacancies in central government-run schools like Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas, which were once considered showcase schools. Only 57 per cent of schools nationally have functional computers, barely over half have internet access, and single-teacher schools, while declining, still exist by the thousands.
Every fan that does not work, every locked toilet, every vacant teacher post that the children in Gaya, Jalore, Alwar, and Fatehpur are protesting is not an isolated failure. It is the lived fallout of the numbers cited above. And the children are standing up and speaking out.
What label do you put on a 10-year-old?
This government is accustomed to defeating political opponents by labelling them. A protester can be called anti-national, urban Naxal, foreign-funded, or, now in Modi’s vocabulary from his latest Independence Day speech, a “dimagi Naxal”—or intellectual Naxal, extending the language of insurgency to any dissenter.
But what label does one apply to a 10-year-old demanding a teacher? What ideology is concealed in a child’s demand for a toilet? What foreign conspiracy lies behind children asking for a working hand pump?
This question goes beyond rhetoric. A state that jails or lathi-charges children in school uniform will have to pay a reputational cost that dwarfs anything it paid for cracking down on college-age protesters, however unfairly. Gen Z could be tear-gassed at Jantar Mantar and the government could still call it law and order, but a state cannot easily send police into a primary school in Alwar without the optics working entirely against it. It is this knowledge that has, so far, pushed district magistrates to show up in person and issue show-cause notices rather than lathis.
A child raised with a broken fan and a clogged toilet does not need years of counter-narrative to see the gap between promise and delivery—the gap is standing in the room with her every day. The state’s usual instruments of persuasion and coercion find less purchase here, not because the children are immune to politics, but because the terrain simply isn’t built for either.
A worrying precedent
This is not an unprecedented phenomenon, and the precedents are not comforting for those in power. The most dramatic example from history is Soweto, 1976, when Black schoolchildren in apartheid South Africa—some as young as 10—marched against the imposition of Afrikaans as the language of instruction. Police opened fire, with a 13-year-old boy, Hector Pieterson, among the first to be killed. The killing of children converted a narrow curricular grievance into a nationwide uprising that spread to over a hundred townships and is now remembered as the turning point that made apartheid’s collapse inevitable. In a near-identical incident, in Birmingham in 1963, thousands of Black schoolchildren marched for desegregation after adult recruitment had stalled; the images of police dogs and fire hoses turned on the children shocked America and helped push through the Civil Rights Act. In both cases, it was not the grievance that made the movement dangerous but the state’s decision to counter children with force.
In India too, we saw a version of the escalation logic. The Gujarat student agitation of 1973-74 began over something as mundane as a rise in hostel food charges. It expanded into a movement against inflation and corruption, forced Chief Minister Chimanbhai Patel to resign, and fed directly into Jayaprakash Narayan’s Bihar movement—a chain of events that eventually shaped the politics of the Emergency itself.
The lesson from all these cases is the same: young people, especially children, puncture political complacency precisely because their grievances cannot be absorbed into the ideological script that governments are built to fight.
Issues unite where identity divides
For decades, Indian politics has been remarkably successful at diverting anger toward questions of religion, caste, nationalism, the cow, and temples. These issues are potent because they divide people horizontally. Education, health, toilets, wages, and competent teachers do something different: they direct anger upward, at the performance of the state itself.
A Hindu and a Muslim may disagree over a temple. But both agree that their children need a working fan in July. A Dalit and an upper-caste farmer may disagree over reservation. But both need their child’s teacher to show up in class. Issues can unite where identity divides—and a state that has spent a decade mastering identity politics may find itself with far fewer tools against a politics of shared, undeniable, measurable failure.
Gen Z demonstrated that the fear of government can be broken. Gen Alpha, without meaning to, without ideology, and without anyone able to discipline them for it, may now be demonstrating what comes next: not a demand for slogans, but a demand that the state simply do its job. History suggests that this is a harder kind of movement to contain and—if the state misjudges it the way Pretoria misjudged Soweto—a more dangerous one to provoke.
Anand Teltumbde is a former CEO of Petronet India Limited (PIL), a professor at IIT Kharagpur and Goa Institute of Management, a civil rights activist, and the author of over 30 books.

Title: Prevent misuse of data by private entities, SC tells government

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday expressed concern about a commercial technological ecosystem which allegedly accesses, retrieves and verifies sensitive individual information on provident fund and income tax returns and told the Centre about the desirability of devising an antidote to the problem with the assistance of domain experts.

Title: Spirit Airlines Wants to Sell Its Data to Google. Former Flight Attendants Are Freaked Out

Spirit Airlines may have declared bankruptcy this spring, but the budget airline is still worth something—to AI giants, at least. In mid-August, Google won a $10 million bid to purchase some 34 years of the airline’s data, from invoices and flight operations information to Wi-Fi sales, employee records, and crew pairings.
In a statement, a Google spokesperson said the data “can be helpful in improving our products and AI models.” The sale would not include customer data, and Google “will not receive any personal information from this dataset,” the spokesperson said. The winning offer, chosen over a competing $7.5 million proposal from AI data and training company Mercor, has to be approved by a judge.
If former Spirit Airlines attendants have their way, that won’t happen easily. Just days after the court announced Google’s winning bid, the labor union representing 5,500 former Spirit Airlines flight attendants filed an objection to the sale. Lawyers for the 55,000-member Association of Flight Attendants (AFA) argue the sale would include an enormous amount of sensitive employee information, and that even Google’s promised safeguards wouldn’t prevent privacy violations of decades of flight attendants who never could have guessed that their data would be sold to train AI systems.
The employee data “has no business being sold,” Sara Nelson, the president of the AFA, said in a written statement to WIRED. “This is outrageous!”
The legal objection opens a potential new front in the AI data wars, as major frontier labs including Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mercor scramble to find new sources of data to help train their products. US laws have contemplated how best to protect consumer data, even after companies go bankrupt and are sold off for parts—laws that have taken on new salience and value in the age of AI.
But the Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ legal objection highlights the gap between data protections for consumers and for workers. It also marks the first public tangle between labor unions and corporations over the sale and use of employee data for AI training purposes, legal experts say.
“There is no boundary between the information and data that the employee is producing and their own personal information. The law has not caught up,” says Seema Patel, a law professor at the University of California, College of the Law, San Francisco, who studies labor issues and technology. (California is one of the few states to have explicit worker data protection laws.) "Companies are having a field day with this.”
In the past few months, startups specializing in selling defunct companies’ data—including old Slack messages, GitHub content, and Google Drives—to those training AI have reportedly made millions. Meanwhile, so-called egocentric data collection efforts are on the rise, as companies race to record humans performing work like cooking meals, cleaning kitchens, and operating factory lines, and use that data to train machines to aid and eventually replace them.
The Spirit data sale would, according to a court filing, include more than 1 million time-card records, over 175,000 employee records, nearly 150,000 employee tax forms, employment contracts and litigation files, 80,000 email accounts, 17 million individually owned Microsoft OneDrive items, 20.6 million shared Microsoft SharePoint files, and 500 million Microsoft Teams records.
The court filing describes a process through which the data buyer—Google—would select or OK a third party to strip the data of elements that could be used to link the information with a particular consumer. A hearing related to the data sale has been delayed to September 9.
One former Spirit Airlines flight attendant called the potential data sale “troubling.” “I knew they were going to sell every single part of consumer data. It never crossed my mind that they would be so bold as to sell our private data for AI,” says the flight attendant, who spoke to WIRED under condition of anonymity because they’re still looking for new employment.
The flight attendant says his and other employees’ email accounts and Microsoft files included deeply sensitive personal and medical information shared with the airline as part of their employment and insurance agreements, detailing everything from miscarriages to incidents of domestic violence to union contract negotiations. “There’s this huge consensus of feeling extremely violated by this,” he says.
In its legal objection, AFA argues that “deidentifying” employee data isn’t the same as providing confidentiality, because AI itself makes it much easier to relink private information across datasets, even without specific names. “The privacy architecture of this transaction is consumer-facing; its payload is disproportionately employee-facing,” the union's lawyers wrote. The union argues the bankruptcy court should either exclude all flight-attendant-related data from the sale or guarantee that employee data receives the same protections as consumer information.
Though the flight attendants’ objections are just a small part of the larger Spirit Airlines bankruptcy proceeding, the outcome could have a major effect on how labor unions and companies think about employee data going forward, says Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California, Irvine, who studies privacy and technology.
“In a world where billions and trillions are being spent on [large language models], anything where words are used is subject to its own profit-making purpose,” he says. “If this goes forward with no limitation, there is no protection for any employee.”
The fact that flight attendants are at the forefront of this labor question, rather than workers who sit at desks and type all day, is a reminder that all employees can create data with market value. “All workers bring an immense amount of knowledge,” Patel says. “Now artificial intelligence has given us the ability to process all different kinds of data.”
More value, meanwhile, is one of the former Spirit Airlines’ flight attendants’ goals. Separately, the union has also intervened in the bankruptcy to demand roughly $68 million in unpaid vacation, health care, and back pay.
“We feel it's another slap in the face that we're waiting for our missing wages while Spirit is going to profit $10 million off our private information,” says the former flight attendant.

Title: From the Apple Cup to the Iron Bowl: The AP’s annual dream college football Top 25 road trip

From the Apple Cup to the Iron Bowl: The AP’s annual dream college football Top 25 road trip
College football’s offseason of discontent is almost over.
If you’re tired of court cases, legislative haggling and uncertainty over who can even be a college athlete, you can look forward to some actual games soon. And with that, it’s time for the AP’s annual attempt to map out college football’s hypothetical dream road trip.
Reviewing the rules:
— We must see every team in the AP’s preseason Top 25 at least once.
— Travel between games must be reasonable in the time available. Long drives and even flights are OK, but if you’re at a night game in Los Angeles, you’re not getting to Penn State for an early afternoon kickoff the next day.
This season’s 17-game journey looks like this:
Washington State at No. 17 Washington (Sept. 6)
Now that these two rivals are no longer in the same conference, the Apple Cup is played early in the season. This year it’s the opener for both teams. Talk about a tone setter.
No. 19 SMU at Florida State (Sept. 7)
Already we’re racking up travel miles. The Apple Cup is in the afternoon, and after hopping a red-eye out of the Pacific Northwest, we arrive in the Florida panhandle with plenty of time for an afternoon nap before the evening kickoff between the Seminoles and Mustangs. An early test for Mike Norvell, who is likely running out of chances at Florida State.
No. 25 Missouri at Kansas (Sept. 11)
The Border War rivalry between these two resumed last year after a hiatus of over a decade. Presumably there will be at least some unity on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.
No. 20 Tennessee at Georgia Tech (Sept. 12)
Again, this a quick turnaround, but doable since the Volunteers and Yellow Jackets kick off at night. Fernando Mendoza’s brother Alberto takes over the quarterbacking at Georgia Tech this season.
No. 11 LSU at No. 9 Mississippi (Sept. 19)
The single easiest game to include on this entire journey: Lane Kiffin’s return to Oxford. Nobody does the fan base-as-scorned-lover routine quite like the SEC.
No. 10 Oklahoma at No. 3 Georgia (Sept. 26)
Between the hedges for the first major test of the season for the Bulldogs. Georgia entered the season in the top five for the eighth straight year.
No. 1 Ohio State at No. 22 Iowa (Oct. 3)
If the top-ranked Buckeyes lose at Texas in September, the pressure will be on to avoid any further slip-ups before Indiana and Oregon pop up on their schedule. That means taking care of business at Iowa.
No. 14 Southern California at No. 18 Penn State (Oct. 10)
This is a good candidate to be Penn State’s annual White Out game — and it’s the first major home test for new Nittany Lions coach Matt Campbell.
No. 1 Ohio State at No. 6 Indiana (Oct. 17)
The Hoosiers rolled to an undefeated season in 2025, but their biggest wins were on the road or at neutral sites. Now the defending champs get a shot at Ohio State in Bloomington. Indiana has certainly earned this stage.
No. 23 Houston at No. 21 Utah (Oct. 24)
With Conner Weigman back at quarterback, Houston is expected to be one of the top teams in the Big 12. The Cougars travel to Utah in late October. By then we’ll have a sense of how the Utes are holding up after the end of the Kyle Whittingham era.
Arizona State at No. 14 BYU (Oct. 31)
After checking out the sights, a second straight weekend in Utah and a chance to watch rushing star LJ Martin and BYU in an intriguing Big 12 matchup.
No. 7 Miami at No. 4 Notre Dame (Nov. 7)
A pair of top-10 teams, neither of which has that many monster games on its schedule. That means this clash is a must-see, although we’ll have to skip Ohio State-Oregon that same day. (We’ll regret this if the Buckeyes and Ducks are still ranked 1-2, but there’s a decent chance that changes before then.)
No. 16 Michigan at No. 2 Oregon (Nov. 14)
The Wolverines and quarterback Bryce Underwood have a wide range of possible outcomes this season, but if they’re in the playoff hunt in mid-November then this game out west becomes a huge one.
Pittsburgh at No. 24 Louisville (Nov. 21)
Pat Narduzzi’s defense against Jeff Brohm’s offense. There could be about eight teams tied for first in the ACC by this point, so this game may have significant implications.
TCU at No. 12 Texas Tech (Nov. 26)
Our journey concludes with a busy final week, starting with a Texas two-step that includes this Thanksgiving showdown.
No. 5 Texas at No. 8 Texas A&M (Nov. 27)
The drive from Lubbock to College Station is over 400 miles, but we’ll make it to Kyle Field for this evening kickoff and a potentially massive rivalry game.
Auburn at No. 13 Alabama (Nov. 28)
Alabama is the last Top 25 team we haven’t seen yet, and an early flight out of Texas helps us reach Bryant-Denny Stadium in time for the Iron Bowl. It’s the first shot at the Crimson Tide for Alex Golesh after taking over as Auburn coach.

Title: India and Pakistan can still find each other across the border

There is a young woman who writes beautifully. Her words touch the heart and resonate in the mind. She has lived all her life in Colaba, Mumbai. Her first name is Sana. My youngest daughter is also named Sana. It is a Semitic word found in all the three great religions of Palestine: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. It derives from the Hebrew word “Hosanna”, which means “praise”: praise to the Creator for the miracle and mystery of birth and life and all that we call Nature. As a given name it is much in contemporary use in the Muslim world. But to find it coupled with a Hindu surname is rare—Krishna in this girl’s case and Aiyar in my daughter’s case.
My daughter is called Sana because she was born in Karachi during my posting there as a diplomat. Her two older sisters had a senior with this name in school whom they greatly admired. That is how our Sana became Sana. In Sana Krishna’s case, neither of her parents is Muslim and she was born in Mumbai. It was her Zoroastrian mother who gave Sana Krishna her first name, adding a fourth religion to those who celebrate hamd-us-sana, “The Glory of God”. She took her surname from her Hindu father.
But it is not her parents of whom she writes, but of her beloved “Dada”, her paternal grandfather who used to ready her for school, then wait in the melting heat for her to emerge from class and carry her back home on his shoulders, regaling her with stories from his lost youth—lost because he was raised in that part of Punjab, in and around Lahore, which became Pakistan. And as a young adult, he had to leave everything behind, including his friends and memories, to save his life.
This rang a bell in my head as I too was born in Lahore, where my Tamil father had lived for 20 years but was forced to reluctantly uproot his life when the country was vivisected.
Sana writes: “I did not think of Dada as a refugee. He was simply my grandfather. His Lahore was simply a place where he had once lived. Partition belonged to history books, black-and-white photographs and stories from another era. Only much later did I begin to understand that the gentleness I associated with him was inseparable from the generation he belonged to.”
Dada had bought a chair for the chowkidar to sit on during the long hours he daily guarded the gates. It is that characteristic of gentleness that she invokes of an era which the rest of us associate with the horrific violence that rent asunder people and their forefathers who had known each other intimately and remembered with great fondness their lives together.
She invokes also their resilience as they rebuilt their lives in lands they had known nothing about: “Who opened the first shop? Who found the first job? Who created recipes from memory?” And poignantly concludes the passage: “Distance has a peculiar way of making inherited histories visible.” I think we have discovered Gen Z’s Arundhati Roy.
She goes on: “Our food is mirrored flavours. Our music is mirrored longings. Our memories are often mirrored landscapes.” Sana regrets our having to interpret “every relationship through a national border” and speculates that “perhaps our responsibility is to stop treating the recognition of shared humanity as a betrayal”.
What she wants her generation to “keep discovering” is “that the stranger on the other side of the border speaks in a voice that sounds unexpectedly like home”.
Jigar Moradabadi had anticipated her:
“Unka jo kaam hai, woh
Ahl-e-siyasat jaane/
Mera paigham mohabbat hai,
Jahan tak pahunche.”
(“Let the politicians, whose job it is,
Get on with it/
My message is Love,
As far as it might spread”)
A senior statesman, much involved with foreign affairs, has refuted the relevance of these sentimentalities. Title: ‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’

‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
The video of a Ukrainian cyclist being targeted and killed by a short-range drone posted – and later deleted – by the Russian military Friday left viewers outraged and shaken. But it’s not the first time that Russian drone operators have been accused of terrorising Ukrainian civilians by deliberately targeting them in “human safaris” denounced as a war crime by an independent UN commission.
First, he freezes, caught off guard. Then the young Ukrainian cyclist begins to backpedal awkwardly, his eyes never leaving the Russian drone that hovers ahead of him. It moves closer, and he swings his leg over the bike and tries to run. He doesn’t make it.
Even though the footage, posted Friday on the official Telegram account of the 3rd Army Corps of the Russian armed forces, cuts off before the moment of impact, the video’s description leaves no doubt of the outcome. The Russian soldiers congratulate themselves on having taken out an “enemy combatant” in the Ukrainian district of Kramatorsk, not far from the front line in the northern Donetsk region.
Two years of ‘human safaris’
But the cyclist was visibly unarmed, wearing civilian clothes and looked like any other young man riding his bike down a country road. Independent Russian media outlet Astra quickly accused the Russian military of trying to pass off an unarmed cyclist as a Ukrainian combatant.
The video spread swiftly across social media as influential accounts, including prominent Kremlin critic and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, reposted the footage to denounce the Russian military’s apparent cruelty.
Less than 48 hours and hundreds of outraged comments later, the 3rd Army Corps took the video down.
It’s far from the first time that Russian drones laden with explosives and controlled from a distance have targeted civilians in Ukraine’s frontline regions. The Ukrainians have even found a term for these deadly drone hunts – “human safaris”.
“On the one hand, I'm very happy that there is more attention on this,” said Olga Tokariuk, a specialist in Ukraine at the British think-tank Chatham House. “On the other hand, this is not something new. This has been happening for two years. And the impunity that Russia faces for these attacks just means it can continue.”

The “human safari” carried out by Russian drone operators seems to have begun in July 2024 in Kherson, a city on the banks of Dnipro River in the country’s south.
“Kherson in 2024 was the point at which isolated incidents developed into a sustained campaign,” said Will Kingston-Cox, a specialist in Russia and the Ukraine war at the International Team for the Study of Security in Verona. “Initially, small quadcopters followed individuals and vehicles and dropped explosives. Since then, we have seen FPV (first-person view) impact drones expanding the practice in scale, frequency and geography. Documented targets include pedestrians, cyclists, private cars, buses, ambulances and rescue workers.”
In Kherson, Russian forces installed on the opposite bank of the Dnipro can easily use short-range drones to target the population who had either remained in or returned to the city following its recapture by the Ukrainian army at the end of 2022.
‘Those seconds are so precious’
Numerous eye-witness accounts, including several reported by FRANCE 24’s Observers team, describe a climate of constant fear of being targeted and killed by a Russian drone.

Tokariuk, who wrote a report on the “human safaris” in 2025, said that people she’d interviewed in Kherson had spoken of being under a state of almost permanent tension.
“Something really striking that they told me was they would only go out there if the weather was bad – because drones cannot really operate in rain or snow or fog,” she said. “And they would also tell me they would drive really fast in their cars, because that maximises your chances of survival if you're hunted by a drone … People wouldn’t use their seatbelts when they're driving, because those seconds are so precious when they see a drone hovering above their car about to hit them, and they need to get out of the car really quickly.”
For its part, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine condemned these “human safaris” as a war crime, for deliberately targeting a civilian population, and a potential crime against humanity, for its possible use as a tool to carry out forcible population transfers.
“They are targeting precisely not only civilians in their day-to-day life, but also hospitals and shops and very basic things that sustain day-to-day life for people,” said Ivan Klyszcz, a specialist in Russia at the Centre of Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia. “So there's definitely a pressure on the civilian population, and inevitably this leads to people to relocate. I cannot say that this is part of a larger plan for population transfer – but it is working out that way.”

The UN commission reported that roughly 150 civilians had been killed and hundreds more wounded in Kherson region by short-range drones since the end of 2024.
Veronika Hinman, a specialist in the Ukraine war at the University of Portsmouth who has studied the use of drones in the conflict, said that while she wasn’t convinced the practice could be described as official army tactics, it certainly seemed tolerated by the military brass.
“I've been trying to think whether this could be just an isolated incident, whether we could consider these drone operators as 'bad apples' or rogue soldiers acting independently – or whether, if you look at the company itself that, they are remnants of an informal militia integrated into Russian forces later on,” she said. “But no, it doesn't seem anything like that. It's not an isolated incident.”
Cutting promos
Although Kherson remains ground zero for this grim practice, the fact that Friday’s cyclist was targeted by a drone in the distant Kramatorsk district shows that these “human safaris” have spread beyond the battered city.
Tokariuk said similar attacks had also been reported in Ukraine’s border region of Sumy, as well as in Kharkhiv, which sits across the border from Russia’s Belgorod region.
She maintained it was impossible that the drone operators didn’t know the people they were targeting were civilians.
“They know exactly what they’re doing,” she said. “The operators of these drones, they can see the real-time footage of who the drone is chasing.”
The practice is also likely a macabre way to train Russian troops to pilot the remote-controlled drones, Hinman said.
“Civilians are not protected. They are easy targets because of what they are wearing, as opposed to soldiers on the battlefield,” she said.

“One of the reasons why they post these on social media, why they make these social media posts, can be to show off what these drones are being used for to the people who fundraise for them,” she said.

“That discrepancy made the video both a propaganda liability and potentially important evidence,” he said. “Operational security concerns cannot be excluded, but reputational and legal containment appears more plausible – particularly because the footage appeared on a channel associated with the army rather than an anonymous pro-war 'miliblogger' (Russian military blogger) account.”
But Tokariuk said she didn’t think the controversy the video had caused would have any real impact on the Russian army’s use of these tactics.
“These drones are cheap to operate – they are flying the distances that they need to,” she said. “In those border regions they use drones because it works. It really keeps civilians in terror. It makes people flee.“
She said the seeming impunity that Russia had enjoyed for more than two years now over its “human safaris” made her worry that other states or actors could start to carry out their own version of the low-cost war crime.
“It is very easy to replicate elsewhere,” she said. “And civilians are completely defenceless against it.”

Title: U.S. removes Syria from state sponsor of terrorism list

The United States on Monday (August 24, 2026) removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, rescinding a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions and marking another step in warming ties between the countries.
The U.S. Department of State also revoked its designation of al-Nusra Front — latterly known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) — as a global terrorist organisation. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.
Rebels led by HTS overthrew long-time Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, with the group's leader, Ahmed al-Sharaa, taking over as president as the country rebuilds after more than 13 years of civil war.
"Today's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Treasury said the moves were "in line with President [Donald] Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria."
But the agency stressed that its removal of restrictions on Syria "does not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable."
Warming ties
HTS was earlier known as al-Nusra Front and was formerly the branch of Al-Qaeda in Syria. It broke ties with the jihadist group in 2016.
Also Read | New beginning: On Syria’s present and future
The United States had initially announced in July its intent to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa.
Mr. Trump met on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Turkey with the Syrian President, a former jihadist who has sought to recast himself as a unifying figure after the toppling of the Assad family, which ruled with an iron fist for a half-century.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday's (August 24) delistings gave Syrians "a path to prosperity."
The action "eliminates the final major barriers for private sector investment in Syria and promotes Syria's economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy," he said in a statement.
Top officials in Damascus hailed the delisting as a major opportunity for the country, still economically devastated after more than a decade of war that rights groups say killed more than half a million people.
Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani described Washington's delisting as a "historic milestone" and said it reflected "the new Syrian state's commitment to international peace and security."
Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a "success for Syrian diplomacy," according to the official news agency SANA.
It "opens a major and long-awaited door to strengthening Syria's integration into the global economic and financial system, attracting investment and modern technologies, and supporting development opportunities."
Central bank chief Safwat Raslan lauded the development, adding that his institution was "working to build a modern and reliable financial system capable of evolving with developments and taking advantage of all opportunities."

Title: Palestinian artist Sliman Mansour, giant of resistance art, dies aged 79

In Pictures
Celebrated artist Sliman Mansour, one of the founding figures of contemporary Palestinian art, has died at the age of 79 after a long illness, his family announced on Monday.
Born in Birzeit, near Ramallah, in 1947, Mansour rose to prominence in the 1970s as part of a generation of Palestinian artists, writers and poets seeking to rebuild a threatened identity through symbols rooted in land and memory. Over more than five decades, his paintings came to embody the story of Palestine: the farmer clinging to his soil, the stone house on a hill, the embroidered thobe and the smile of a young girl carrying the hope of return.
Mansour studied art in Beirut and Washington and went on to exhibit extensively, both in solo shows and group exhibitions across the Arab world and internationally. His works are held in museums and private collections worldwide, and he received numerous awards in recognition of his contribution to Arab and Palestinian culture.
His visual language drew deeply from the region’s ancient civilisations – Canaanite, Pharaonic and Assyrian – as well as Islamic and Arab art, particularly calligraphy and geometric motifs. Title: Following the questions where they lead

Ever since she was a child playing on her family’s farmland in Wisconsin, Bailey Flanigan was guided by her own selective, yet wide-ranging, curiosity. Describing her young self as spirited and a bit unruly, she directed her energies to everything from building booby traps to doing experimental construction projects to exploring an intense interest in medicine to writing fiction and music to planning nonprofit organizations to help lessen social inequality.
By high school, Flanigan was intensely drawn to particular subjects.
“I found myself unmotivated to take all the AP [advanced placement] classes for the sake of it. My interest was captured by classes where I could be creative — where I could use math to solve real-world problems, creatively write, make music, connect distant ideas, or deeply explore the humanities — and I worked on such classes obsessively, as an opportunity to explore my intuitions and interests,” she says. “Instead of joining clubs, I ended up spending a lot of time thinking and creating on my own, and trying to understand what I enjoyed.”
Today Flanigan is a shared faculty member between the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing and the MIT departments of Political Science and Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and a principal investigator in the MIT Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems. She has been involved in research at the University of Wisconsin, the National Institutes of Health, Google, and Carnegie Mellon, Drexel, Harvard, Princeton, and Stanford universities. Her current work focuses on using computational and mathematical tools to create new avenues for meaningful democratic participation.
Perhaps not surprisingly, her path has crossed huge expanses of subject matter and specialties — from medicine and bioengineering to public health, and from economics to her joint appointment at MIT in computer science and political science, which began in fall 2025.
“My trajectory across disciplines was just a result of me chasing down the problems I felt were most pressing or inspiring at the time. Along the way, I wound up in a lot of situations where I was less well-trained or qualified in the standard ways. While this was sometimes precarious, it was also incredibly fun, and it cultivated my ability to learn the languages of new disciplines more easily — a skill pretty much essential to my current research and job.”
In college at the University of Wisconsin at Madison, Flanigan worked in a wet lab on therapeutic targets in cancer and computationally on tumor genetics. She says she found the research intellectually interesting, but eventually began to wonder about whether it would have the kind of impact she wanted.
“At the time, I started to worry that the science I was developing might only, in the best case, be used by a small, relatively wealthy fraction of the world, when there were people suffering from much more-preventable diseases in much larger numbers,” she says.
So Flanigan moved toward public health, where she researched microfluidic devices for HIV detection that could be used in low-resource settings. Still bothered by the circumstances driving these settings’ limited resources to begin with, she then started to dabble in economics.
Around the same time, Flanigan’s academic advisors were chipping away at preconceptions she held about her own abilities.
Steven Wright, a professor of law and creative writing at UW-Madison, served as Flanigan’s informal mentor throughout college, and they worked together on a case at the Wisconsin Innocence Project.
“He guided me through my evolving interests in science, social inequality, and economics,” she says. “He was one of the people most responsible for convincing me that I could aim higher in my career, and that I could actually go to places like MIT or Harvard.”
Also while she was in college, the two heads of the UW-Madison scholarship office, Debbie Berger and Julie Stubbs, sent Flanigan repeated emails, encouraging her to apply for a Goldwater Scholarship.
“I kept deleting their emails, thinking they were spam — I didn’t think I was the kind of person that would apply for something like that. Their persistence convinced me to apply, and in the process, the horizons I perceived for myself started to change,” she says.
After graduating from UW-Madison, Flanigan worked as a predoctoral research assistant in economics at Princeton. There, Professor Evita Nestoridi, now an associate professor at Stony Brook University, also provided a pivotal moment of support, letting Flanigan audit her real analysis class.
“Evita’s class was my first real exposure to formal mathematics and proofs, and I loved it so much that it completely changed my career trajectory,” Flanigan says. “Despite my initial doubts, she convinced me that I could do math at the graduate level; because of her encouragement, I applied to computer science PhD programs the subsequent fall.”
Choosing Carnegie Mellon for her PhD, Flanigan began research on social choice and democratic decision-making, serving her dual passions for technical research and the issue of “who gets what and why,” she says, quoting Nobel Prize-winning economist Al Roth.
Flanigan has developed algorithms that randomly choose participants of citizens’ assemblies, designed for the common case where willing participants self-select in ways that do not reflect the larger population. In a policy brief, Flanigan gave a hypothetical example of an assembly on artificial intelligence, whose willing participants might skew toward younger, more educated citizens with an interest in technology, leaving other groups underrepresented despite their stake in the issue. The tools Flanigan has developed help balance representation with such features of the selection process as equality among individuals’ chances to participate, resistance to manipulation of the process, and transparency — all of which can affect the general perception of a decision-making group’s legitimacy.
Flanigan’s work is now deployed on panelot.org, a widely used open-access website hosting algorithms for randomly selecting citizen assembly participants.
“The site basically walks practitioners through a series of otherwise very technical trade-offs, making those trade-offs legible and then optimizing according to the priorities practitioners dictate,” she says.
Flanigan says she is motivated to improve how the public makes political decisions, “because if any political solution is going to be viable, the public needs to feel that it was arrived at via a legitimate political process — at least under the forms of government I find most appealing.”
Beyond her work on citizens’ assemblies, Flanigan’s research is exploring new avenues related to how to more systematically get public input on complex decisions, and how the format of questions we ask people in preference elicitation contexts can affect the substance of what we conclude.
“I feel so lucky to be studying these questions from within both political science and EECS, because I have the freedom to explore both the political and technical substance of tools for more direct governance as deeply as I want,” she says.
Flanigan’s curiosity-driven journey through widely varying terrain feels right in the MIT environment, she says.
“From the beginning, I got this sense of belonging at MIT — like my ways of thinking and problem-solving, which had seemed peculiar in many situations, actually made me belong more,” she says. “This was a super refreshing feeling, and it has been 100 percent borne out since I arrived.”
