Title: ICE agent accused of shooting man and lying about it could be freed from Texas jail

An ICE agent accused of shooting a man through the front door of a Minneapolis home and then lying about what happened could be released from a Texas jail Thursday unless a federal judge intervenes.
Christian Castro, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, faces assault and false reporting charges in Minnesota stemming from the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.
Minnesota authorities have sought Castro's extradition since his arrest, but he remains jailed in Brownsville, Texas, near the Mexican border.
Under Texas law, Castro must be released after 90 days in custody unless the legal situation changes. That deadline arrives Thursday.
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison have sued to force Texas to turn Castro over and to prevent the Cameron County sheriff from releasing him while the extradition dispute continues.
Prosecutors allege Castro fired through the front door of a Minneapolis home, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg. The bullet ultimately lodged in the wall of a child's bedroom.
Authorities further allege Castro falsely claimed afterward that Sosa-Celis and another man had attacked an ICE officer with a broom handle and snow shovel.
During a federal court hearing Tuesday in Brownsville, attorneys for Minnesota warned that getting Castro back to face charges could become significantly more difficult if he is released — particularly if he leaves the jurisdiction.
U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. said he was inclined not to block the Cameron County sheriff from releasing Castro but expected to decide Wednesday on Minnesota's request for a temporary restraining order.
Lawyers representing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott argued that Minnesota's lawsuit is premature because Abbott has not formally approved or rejected its extradition request.
“I think ripeness is a significant issue,” Rodriguez said.
Abbott has ordered a state review into whether Castro legally qualifies as a “fugitive.” His general counsel, Trevor W. Ezell, has also questioned whether a court has the authority to impose a deadline on the governor for deciding an extradition request.
Minnesota disputes the need for further investigation.
“There’s nothing legally left for them to investigate,” Kimberly Ann Svendsen, an attorney representing the Minnesota attorney general, told the court.
Abbott said last week he would not respond to Minnesota's extradition request, citing ongoing investigations into alleged fraud involving government social service programs in the state. Trump has previously cited those investigations while defending his administration's immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

Title: Told Vijay Mekedatu dam is in Tamil Nadu's best interest: Shivakumar on Cauvery row

Told Vijay, Mekedatu dam is in Tamil Nadu's best interest: DK Shivakumar on Cauvery row

Title: Knives, pistols and ‘aura farming’: Inside Delhi’s teen ‘gangs’

They’re too young to be tried as adults. That’s exactly why gangs in North-East Delhi want them.
In the cramped, winding lanes of North-East Delhi, boys are picking up knives and country-made pistols before they ever pick up a schoolbook.
Step behind the main roads here and you find a world of the underage offender. Armed with blades and homemade firearms, they don’t just spread fear, some of them deal in death. For months, we walked these lanes, day and night, tracking down the hideouts where these stories begin. We tried to trace the pattern behind each incident, and we sought out the young people who have become part of this world.
Few outsiders ever see this side of North-East Delhi up close. For a striking number of young people here, drifting into a gang and into crime isn’t the exception, it's simply what happens. Most of the time, these stories surface only as a headline in the next day’s paper, then disappear. What draws children toward this life? Is it the neighbourhood they grow up in? Or is it that the system itself never gave them another road to take?
The boys who are already part of this world talk about it almost casually, roaming the streets, and smoking. “We get our knives, our katta [country-made pistols], our pistols from our bade bhai [elder brothers],” they say, but they won’t give up their names. Our reporting found established gangsters, some behind bars, some still free, who supply the weapons and the ammunition and hand out small rewards in return to these underage offenders.
Vinay Tyagi, who spent roughly 15 years in the Crime Branch and the Special Cell covering North-East Delhi, said, “Easy money is the first draw. The second is that the big players, whether they’re locked up or free, actively recruit minors, because the Juvenile Justice Act caps their maximum sentence at three years, no matter the charge. Larger gangs bring these boys in on purpose. And once they’re in, they have their own bills to pay and quotas to meet.”

Title: Japan to Unveil New Oil Diversification Strategy

Japan is today set to announce an energy import diversification plan that will include stipulations about support for pipelines in the Middle East aimed at diverting export oil flows away from the Strait of Hormuz.
The plan also features a push to reduce the country’s reliance on oil and gas overall, and also reduce its reliance on Middle Eastern oil and gas specifically, Reuters has reported, citing Japanese media. The government also plans to make energy companies share the higher costs of importing crude from places other than the Middle East.
Before the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran broke out, Japan relied on the Middle East for almost all of its crude oil imports, which are vital for the resource-poor country. After the war, the Japanese government rushed to secure alternative suppliers. These include the United States, Canada, African oil producers, and Azerbaijan.
This diversification has carried a hefty price tag, however. Last month, Japan’s total import bill hit an all-time high of $76.39 billion because of higher international oil prices. That monthly import figure beat the previous record set a month earlier, suggesting this month’s import bill could be record-breaking as well.
Japan is also one of the world’s biggest LNG importers, and earlier this summer reduced gas-fired generation in favor of coal as the price of liquefied natural gas remained elevated. Japan has been burning more coal and less gas for power generation since the war in the Middle East started, and it is not the only one. Many Asian countries have been forced to make the switch from gas to coal on affordability and availability grounds.
In addition to all this, Japan, like others, made several crude oil releases from strategic storage to weather the impact of the war on its energy security and economy. This, however, has left strategic reserves depleted and in need of replenishment, which will be problematic as the Middle East crisis continues.

Title: Global economy in tug-of-war between oil shock and AI boom: IMF chief

The global economy has weathered the oil shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz "better than feared" due to various factors, including an investment boom in artificial intelligence, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva has said.
“What started out as a U.S. phenomenon with AI is now becoming a growth engine for the global economy, with other countries ramping up construction of data centres and other infrastructure,” Ms. Georgieva told journalists on Tuesday (August 25, 2026).
She said the global economy had “weathered the energy shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz better than we feared” due to a combination of factors, including drawdowns of oil and gas reserves and increases in non-Gulf supply.
“And it is enjoying the tailwinds from an AI investment boom, most notably in the U.S., where both corporate earnings and consumer demand remain strong,” Ms. Georgieva said ahead of the G-20 finance ministerial meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, next week.
She said the global economy was witnessing a tug-of-war between the negative supply shock from West Asia and the positive demand shock from AI.
“The net impact of these two forces is asymmetric across countries and depends on their exposure to energy disruptions, macroeconomic vulnerabilities, and their position in the AI chain,” Ms. Georgieva said.
Ms. Georgieva said risks to the outlook were more balanced than around the Spring Meetings but remained tilted to the downside, while uncertainty remained high.
“Mounting fiscal pressures, as evidenced by rising bond yields, and a stalled disinflation process are sources of worry for both markets and policymakers,” she said.
The IMF chief said oil and gas reserves were shrinking and the northern hemisphere winter would arrive before long.
“This means the energy shock is not over: a renewed rise in oil prices could fuel inflation, forcing central banks to retain a restrictive policy stance, with knock-on implications for debt service and economic activity,” she said.
Ms. Georgieva said the future impact of AI remained subject to significant uncertainties, including possible risks to financial stability.
“Should the outlook deteriorate, it will further widen the dispersion of growth prospects around the world. Some countries, especially low-income countries that depend on fuel imports, are already in a tough spot,” she said.
For low-income countries, disruptions in the supply of oil, gas and other key commodities such as fertiliser could translate into food insecurity, a problem potentially exacerbated by extreme weather, Ms. Georgieva said.
“The risk of falling behind on AI is also more prominent in the developing world,” she said.
In July, the IMF lowered its 2026 global growth forecast to 3%, warning of downside risks from the West Asia conflict, trade fragmentation and uncertainties surrounding artificial intelligence.
The institution's next revision of its growth outlook is due in mid-October during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Parton donated $1 million to vaccine research at Vanderbilt University in 2020, making her an early sponsor of Moderna’s vaccine development.
She conducted a literacy program for preschool children across the United States, as well as in Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Ireland, and provided scholarships to high school students in the Tennessee county where she was born.
The county erected a life-size statue of her in front of the courthouse in thanks, though she declined another proposed statue of her in Nashville in 2021, saying, “Given all that’s going on in the world, I don’t think putting me on a pedestal is appropriate at this time.”
It was this ability to stay true to her roots, combined with her drive to work hard and her nonpartisanship, that fueled her appeal among conservatives and liberals in a politically polarised America.

Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946, in Pittman Centre, Tennessee, and grew up in a one-room cabin in nearby Locust Ridge. One of 12 children of tobacco farmer Robert Lee Parton, her difficult childhood gave credibility to her often personal songs trilled in a distinctive soprano.

She penned her hit song “I Will Always Love You” as a farewell to Wagoner when she decided to pursue a solo career.
On the first day Parton arrived in country music’s capital, she met Carl Dean, an asphalt paver. They would marry two years later, in 1966. Throughout their long marriage, Dean shunned the spotlight and did not tour with her, though he would be a muse for many of her greatest hits, including “Jolene,” which was inspired by a red-haired bank teller’s crush on Dean.
‘The Dolly image’
Her own appearance was the object of intense interest. Initially embarrassed, she eventually found the humor in frequent questions about her extravagant dress sense and generous figure.
She dismissed rumours that her breasts were insured and laughed off periodic rumours that she was bedridden due to their weight, telling People magazine: “Well, they are heavy, but they haven’t crippled me yet.”
Parton patterned her signature look on a woman she would see walking around her Tennessee hometown in tight skirts and high heels, with red nails, red lipstick and peroxided hair. “I thought she was beautiful. But everybody said, ‘She’s trash!’” Parton wrote in her 2023 book “Behind the Seams: My Life in Rhinestones.” “I laughed and said, ‘Well, if that’s trash, that’s what I want to be when I grow up!’” But as much as she embraced her signature look, she also viewed it as distinct from herself. “I look one way and am another,” she told Ladies’ Home Journal in 1982. “It makes for a good combination. I always think of ‘her,’ the Dolly image, like a ventriloquist does his dummy. I have fun with it. I think, what will I do with her this year to surprise people? What’ll she wear? What’ll she say?”
She also expressed the wish that her appearance would serve to sell, rather than overshadow, her talent.

Her music gained a following not only among the public but also among fellow singers who widely covered her songs — perhaps most famously Whitney Houston’s rendition of “I Will Always Love You.” Some of Parton’s most beloved covers and duets were with her goddaughter, American pop star Miley Cyrus, and Cyrus’ father, country music star Billy Ray Cyrus.
“Jolene” was covered by artists as varied as Beyoncé and The White Stripes.
While Parton was a force on stage and an accomplished vocalist, what set her apart from her peers was her talent with words. Parton wrote every one of her hit songs. All told, she penned an estimated 3,000 throughout her life, though she recorded only about 450 of them.
“I love to write poetic songs and sing flowery words,” she wrote in “Dolly Parton, Songteller.” “I like to make you see something visually, so I want to paint a picture. And I love to come up with clever lines, not just like a songwriter, but like a poet.”

Parton made her movie debut in the 1980s in “9 to 5,” starring alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin, with the title tune earning Parton an Oscar nomination for songwriting. She got another Oscar songwriting nomination in 2006 for “Travelin’ Thru,” written for the film “Transamerica.”
Her other movie acting roles included “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas,” “Steel Magnolias,” “Rhinestone” and “Straight Talk.”
Twenty-five of her songs reached No. 1 on the Billboard Country charts, and she was a member of the Songwriters Hall of Fame, receiving its highest honour, the Johnny Mercer Award, in 2007. She was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2022.
Parton received her first Grammy Award in 1978 for her song “Here You Come Again.” In 1988, she won the People’s Choice Award for favorite all-around female entertainer.
But despite all her accolades and achievements, Parton found the greatest meaning in her art.
“I feel like I’m closest to God when I write,” she wrote in “Dolly Parton, Songteller.” “A great line will just come to me, and I’ll go, ‘Hey, thank You, Lord. I know I didn’t think of that.’”
“At the end of the day, I hope that I will be remembered as a good songwriter. The songs are my legacy.”

Title: How Capital Markets Finance Protects Balance Sheet Returns

An insurer settles a claim months after the loss. An asset manager marks someone else's fund at day's end. The sell side doesn't get that grace period. A capital markets CFO can't wait for quarter-end to see where return on the balance sheet landed that—that balance sheet carries market, funding, and liquidity risk continuously, priced position by position, all day.
Before the desk has time to react, the ground can shift under it: the financing cost on a position that was priced correctly last week, the capital consumed by that position as exposures move, or a funding gap opening faster than anticipated. Each number comes out of a different system — desk P&L, treasury funding curves, risk engines weighing exposure against netting sets and margin — and each is increasingly shaped by AI-informed pricing, funding, and risk workflows that reach across all of them.
The sell side runs on its balance sheet. As markets move and spreads shift, funding costs, capital consumption, and liquidity demands move with them, each shaping how efficiently the firm can deploy scarce balance sheet and generate returns. Helping the business understand those tradeoffs and protect profitability has long been finance's job.
That job has gotten harder. Volatility is up, trading books turn over faster, and Basel III Endgame together with the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB) raise the capital required to support market risk. Industry analyses have warned that the FRTB standardized approach can materially affect market-risk capital requirements, depending on portfolio composition, jurisdiction, and modeling approach. Finance sits at the center of it, translating an increasingly complex set of funding, capital, and liquidity decisions for trading, treasury, and leadership.
Now add AI agents embedded in pricing workflows, funding recommendations, reporting, surveillance, and other processes across the trading book. It isn't only that AI is informing more decisions, its that those decisions now touch funding, capital, liquidity, and valuation at the same time, and the pace of that shift will keep accelerating.
Markets, spreads, and funding move all day. Finance protects balance sheet returns as they do, but doing so increasingly requires a shared language for what those numbers actually mean.
Finance is good at finding the number, even buried in complexity. But a good finance team is also the first to say the number alone doesn't tell the story. What matters is what's behind it: the definitions, the desks and products, the funding and spread drivers, and how each is shifting as the business moves.
That's the job of an ontology: capturing meaning and keeping it current as the business changes. On the sell side, meaning is inseparable from the firm’s own balance sheet—a position isn’t just a number, it's capital consumed, funding drawn, and risk the desk is carrying until it's hedged or unwound.
For capital markets, firms can anchor that context in established standards such as FIBO, the Financial Industry Business Ontology, which defines how desks, products, and instruments relate to one another in terms a risk or finance system can reason over. Paired with the firm’s governed data and business definitions, that context lets finance read a number the same way across front office, treasury, risk, and regulatory reporting.
Accurate is the right figure. Correct is the same figure, rooted in the desk, the market, and the funding.
An ontology holds up if it's kept current, though. Markets don’t wait for quarterly metadata updates, so context has to move as fast as the business itself.
This is where Genie comes in—Databricks’ suite of data-smart AI coworkers, grounded in enterprise context. Genie One helps finance leaders ask direct questions, investigate trusted business data, and carry that understanding into the next step of their work, pulling together the relevant definitions, desks, positions, source data, and permissions that matter. The goal isn't a readout of what happened; its an informed discussion of what to do next. People stay accountable for pricing, funding, risk, and capital decisions.
That's not hypothetical. One top global bank, was untangling this fragmentation problem across multiple data sources and reporting standards; it cut regulatory data processing time for liquidity reporting from 10 hours to 8 minutes, letting Treasury respond faster as market conditions changed.
Three questions sit on the mind of every capital markets finance team, each feeding into the next. Here's how Genie changes the work on each one.
Where will funding and liquidity tighten before the desk sees it?
When markets move or inventory builds, funding needs, intraday liquidity, and leverage ratio headroom can shift quickly. Rather than waiting for a periodic report to surface the problem, finance can use Genie One to trace intraday funding usage and collateral movements back to specific positions, desks, and trades driving the change while there's still time to respond.
Where are returns quietly eroding?
This one is harder to catch because it often happens a few basis points at a time: funding costs creep up, spreads compress, or the capital required against a position increases. Genie One helps finance follow the erosion to its source — the desks, products, positions, funding lines, and capital drivers behind it — instead of noticing it only after it shows up in a monthly readout.
Can we explain every capital and valuation number on demand?
A number finance can't stand behind is a number it can't act on, and the moment that gets tested is usually the moment a regulator, auditor, or board member asks. Here Genie One does something slightly different from the first two cases: it surfaces the source data, business definitions, models, and permissions behind a figure on request, so finance has the evidence ready before being asked for it.
Three questions. Three different failure modes. One balance sheet holding all of them together.
Genie One is built for the decision that comes after the analysis: rebalance funding and collateral, protect profitability, or defend a number under scrutiny. The accountable leader still makes the call—Genie One's job is to make sure the questions, context, and follow-up work keep pace with how fast the market is moving.
Protecting the balance sheet isn't new for finance. What's changed is how fast markets, regulation, and now AI reshape the decisions sitting behind it—which means the context finance works from has to move at that same speed. Genie One is built to turn governed business context into trusted analysis and coordinated next steps, so finance isn't always a step behind the number.

What is changing for finance in capital markets?
More of the workflows that inform decisions affecting the balance sheet—inventory pricing, funding, and capital—are increasingly AI-enabled. Finance’s mission to protect return on the balance sheet is unchanged; what has grown is the speed and complexity of change, which finance tools must understand and govern.
Does Genie make pricing, funding, or capital decisions?
No. Those calls belong to the desks, treasury, and risk. Genie One helps authorized finance users investigate governed business data, understand a developing risk earlier, and coordinate with the owners who make the decision.
Why do ontology and governance matter to a capital markets CFO?
Ontology captures what the numbers mean for your business and keeps that context current, so an answer is correct and not just accurate. Governance helps ensure the data and context behind an answer are accessed according to approved permissions and can be investigated when a regulator, auditor, or business leader asks. Together, they give finance a stronger foundation for making and explaining decisions.
What does Genie's ontology understand about capital markets specifically?
Genie One can be grounded in the capital-markets concepts, data, and business definitions that finance teams use, including risk-weighted assets, funding spreads, initial and variation margin, and netting sets. Firms can use standards such as FIBO alongside their own governed business definitions to model relationships among desks, products, instruments, and exposures.
How is Genie different from an AI dashboard or BI tool?
A dashboard shows you what the data says. AI/BI Genie supports natural-language exploration of governed data. Genie One extends that foundation as a data-smart AI coworker, helping users investigate a question, create outputs, and coordinate follow-up work using unified enterprise context. People remain accountable for business decisions.

Title: Railways to quadruple capacity across 11,000 km of key routes carrying 41% of traffic

New Delhi: Indian Railways has embarked on an ambitious plan to quadruple capacity on its seven high-density routes, which together account for about 41% of the national railway network’s traffic despite covering only 16% of its total route length.
Outlining the plan in an Instagram post, railway minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the entire 11,000-km high-density network will be expanded to four tracks. The upgrade is aimed at easing severe congestion along the busiest passenger and freight corridors and preparing for future traffic growth.
The seven high-density routes identified by the railways connect major economic centres and metropolitan regions. They include Delhi-Howrah, Howrah-Chennai, Chennai-Mumbai, Mumbai-Delhi, Delhi-Chennai, Mumbai-Howrah and Delhi-Guwahati.
The concentration of traffic on these corridors makes capacity augmentation particularly important. With these routes carrying nearly half of the railway’s traffic on a relatively small portion of the network, adding additional lines could allow the national transporter to run more passenger and freight services without having to rely solely on improvements in train operations.
The four-laning programme would effectively create four railway lines across these high-density routes, providing greater flexibility for segregating or managing passenger and freight movement. It could also help reduce congestion and improve the ability of the railways to accommodate additional services as demand rises.
Parts of the 11,000-km network already have four tracks, while expansion work is underway across larger stretches. The minister noted that only a small portion of the identified routes is still going through the detailed project report (DPR) approval process, with construction set to begin soon.
The move comes against the backdrop of the railways’ broader push to expand freight capacity and shift more transport activity to trains. Higher capacity on key trunk routes is particularly important as the national transporter seeks to increase freight volumes while continuing to expand passenger services.
Vaishnaw said in the social media post, “If we compare roads with railways, then the railways are 90% cleaner from an environmental point of view and cost a lot less than road transportation. The average cost of moving goods through railways is around ₹1.6 per tonne per km, whereas the same for roadways is about ₹3.6 per tonne per km. So, if we have to reduce the cost of logistics in our country and make our transportation green as our economy grows, we must ensure that all these rail corridors are quadrupled so that the capacity increases.”
The government has in recent years invested heavily in dedicated freight corridors and network expansion to improve the movement of goods. The completion of the eastern and western dedicated freight corridors has already created dedicated capacity on two major freight axes. The proposed four-laning of high-density routes could complement this infrastructure by strengthening capacity on the wider network and improving connectivity between major consumption and production centres.
For freight customers, additional rail capacity could also help reduce logistics costs by providing greater availability and reliability of services. For passengers, the expansion could enable more trains and better scheduling on routes where demand has consistently outpaced available capacity.
The scale of the proposed programme, however, means execution is critical. Four-laning thousands of kilometres of heavily used railway lines will require substantial investment, land availability, engineering work and careful management of existing train operations. Much of the work will have to be undertaken while keeping the existing network operational.
The four-laning plan is therefore likely to become a key component of the railways’ long-term capacity expansion strategy. By focusing investment on routes that carry a disproportionate share of traffic, the national transporter is seeking to address its most pressing capacity constraints while creating headroom for future passenger and freight growth.

Title: Overreaching causal language in the social sciences

Across the social sciences, many studies use cross-sectional designs that reveal associations but are generally unable to support direct causal claims, yet authors of such articles may make or imply causal claims anyway. Here, to examine the prevalence of such ‘overreaching’ causal language, we analysed 194,631 cross-sectional articles using large language models. Over the period 1980–2024, an average of 46% of articles contained causal language in their titles or abstracts, where the annual rate has risen almost threefold since 2000 from 20% to 60%. To examine the effects of such language, we conducted a human-subjects experiment (N = 1, 105), finding that readers frequently indicate abstracts with this phrasing provide causal evidence but that methodological labels (β = −0.4, 95% confidence interval −0.56 to −0.19) and associational wording (β = −0.3, 95% confidence interval −0.43 to −0.07) reduce this tendency. Experiments with five LLMs revealed that model summaries of these articles (N = 100 each) can amplify causal overstatement, removing hedges and introducing causal claims where articles used strictly associational phrasing; however, prompting caution diminishes this pattern.
That is from a recent paper by Calvin Isch, Timothy Dörr, Neil Fasching, Grace Jennings & Duncan J. Watts. Note that Isch is on the job market this year, working with Tetlock and Watts.

Title: When privacy becomes a wall of secrecy

Consider an ordinary civic failure. A road outside a neighbourhood is repaired before the monsoon. Within weeks, it breaks apart. Residents suspect the use of substandard material and want to know the name of the contractor who did the work, who approved the bill, and whether public funds were released after due inspection. They file an application under the Right to Information Act, 2005. The reply comes back: the names and associated records constitute “personal information” and cannot be disclosed. The potholes remain. The file disappears behind privacy.
This is the everyday democratic danger to which the digital rights lawyer Apar Gupta draws attention. When a newly repaired road outside one’s home begins to crumble, and the municipal authorities refuse to respond, the RTI Act offers citizens a definitive means of seeking accountability. It allows them to ask who received the contract, who approved the work, and how public funds were spent.
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP), 2023, Gupta cautions, could obstruct precisely this chain of accountability by denying citizens access to information about “the person who did the work with your money—public money”. What begins as a pothole outside one’s home thus raises a much larger democratic question: can privacy be invoked to conceal the identities and decisions of those entrusted with public authority and public funds?
The controversy turns on a single clause. Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act replaces the carefully qualified exemption in Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act with the phrase: “information which relates to personal information”. The earlier clause protected genuinely private information but permitted disclosure when a larger public interest justified it. It also said that information that could not be denied to Parliament or State legislatures should not be denied to a citizen.
The exemptions have disappeared from Section 8(1)(j). The change potentially transforms privacy from a right protecting citizens against centralised authority into a justification for shielding governments from citizens. While medical histories, family details, and sensitive financial documents deserve protection, the identity of an official in a public office, the name of a contractor paid from public funds, or records showing why an eligible family lost its ration entitlement do not need to be withheld. Their public significance cannot be denied merely by attaching the label “personal”.
Transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj calls the amendment “a huge blow to our ability as citizens to hold the government accountable”. Her warning is rooted in how RTI actually works. The law is not used only by professional activists. Pensioners use it to trace delayed payments; students seek marks and selection records; employees track unpaid wages; families excluded from welfare rolls ask who deleted their names. In such cases, personal data and administrative accountability are often inseparable.
The government disputes the charge that the amendment destroys transparency. Electronics and Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has argued that the DPDP framework balances privacy with the right to information. The government has also pointed to Section 3 of the Act, which exempts information already made publicly available by a person legally obliged to publish it.
However, this justification is circular. A significant amount of government information is made public precisely because the RTI Act compels disclosure. If the amended exemption prevents disclosure at the threshold, the information never becomes “publicly available” and cannot benefit from Section 3. Proactive dissemination by governmental bodies could mitigate this issue; India’s record of compliance with Section 4 of the RTI Act remains uneven.
There exists a significant legal nuance. Section 8(2) of the RTI Act, which serves as a general override allowing disclosure when public interest surpasses the detriment to safeguarded interests, remains intact. The government may argue that this preserves the balancing exercise. However, removing the specific safeguards from Section 8(1)(j) still lowers the first barrier to refusal. An information officer can merely classify a record as personal, forcing an ordinary applicant to undertake a prolonged appeal to invoke the broader public-interest provision. Rights delayed through procedure are frequently rights denied in practice.
The Hyderabad-based policy studies scholar S. Abhiram argues that the policy challenge is to distinguish genuinely private information from that information which concerns the exercise of public authority. Data protection, he observes, should safeguard citizens against intrusive data collection without providing public institutions with an administrative shortcut to withhold information about official decisions and public expenditure.
Privacy vs transparency
For journalists, the danger extends beyond access to government documents. The DPDP Act lacks a clear, overarching exemption for journalistic activities conducted in the public interest. Reporting routinely involves gathering, archiving, verifying, and publishing information about identifiable people—often without their consent, especially when the individual in question is influential and the evidence reveals misconduct.
Delhi-based independent journalist Shubhangi Derhgawen voices the apprehension: “You won’t be able to question those in power”. Veteran journalist Paranjoy Guha Thakurta describes the change more starkly, saying it “rips away our Right to Information”. The Act does not automatically impose a penalty merely because a journalist names a person. Penalties arise from adjudicated breaches of statutory duties. However, the lack of well-defined journalistic protection, combined with potentially significant institutional penalties, creates uncertainty, which can deter small newsrooms and independent journalists.
The constitutional dispute is now before the Supreme Court. Petitions filed by RTI campaigners and journalistic organisations challenge Section 44(3), the absence of adequate public-interest protections, the broad state exemptions, and the institutional autonomy of the Data Protection Board. At the August 7 hearing, petitioners argued that the amendment could impede investigative journalism and place welfare, disciplinary, and public-contract records beyond scrutiny. Chief Justice Surya Kant remarked that “the balance has to be worked out with the right to privacy”. The Union said it would justify the law on record, “subject to judicial review”. The matter is still unresolved.
Balance means not choosing transparency over privacy or privacy over transparency in every case. Both rights respond to the same democratic problem: unequal power. Privacy prevents the government and corporations from making citizens permanently visible; RTI prevents the state from making itself permanently invisible. A legitimate data-protection law must accomplish both.
Parliament can repair the conflict. It should restore an explicit public-interest criterion to Section 8(1)(j), maintain the Parliament exception, distinguish information on private life from information about public duties, and establish a defined exception for journalism, research, whistleblowers, and civic accountability. Public authorities must also proactively disclose contracts, decision-making processes, and welfare criteria in anonymised or minimally intrusive forms wherever possible.
For citizens, this is not an abstract quarrel. It is a basic question about whether and when public money produces private gain and public loss, and whether the citizen will be allowed to ask who was responsible for it.
Madhavi Ravikumar teaches at Department of Communication, University of Hyderabad. Anees. M is a PhD scholar at the Department of Communication, University of Hyderabad.

Title: Oil Prices Fall as Iran-Oman Talks Fuel Hopes of Strait Reopening

Crude oil prices dipped earlier today following news reports about Iran and Oman renewing their talks about joint management of the Strait of Hormuz, as those reports were taken to mean the waterway could soon reopen for normal traffic.
Reuters reported that the two were discussing “a joint temporary navigational corridor” and clearing the strait of mines. As a result, Brent crude was trading at $86.69 per barrel at the time of writing, with West Texas Intermediate at $80.61 per barrel at the time of writing. Traders appear to have shrugged off the latest U.S. sanctions against Iran aimed at squeezing its oil trade even further.
ING commodity analysts wrote in a note earlier today that a Pakistani statement of progress on peace talks had also contributed to the downward pressure on crude. They were, however, cautious about any expectations of a swift return to normal in the Persian Gulf.
“Any agreement between these two parties [Iran and Oman] does not mean we will see normalisation in oil flows through the key chokepoint,” Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote. “We would likely need to see the US lift its blockade on Iranian ports and ease sanctions on Iran before we see any move towards normalisation.”
Meanwhile, tanker tracking data from Windward showed just one vessel traversing the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, a Barbados-flagged LPG carrier that entered the strait. No outbound tanker traffic was recorded for the 24-hour period, the firm said. The tanker moved in dark mode, the data also showed.
“The US claims that an average of 8-9m b/d of oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz, which may be achievable over short time periods,” ING’s Patterson and Manthey also wrote. “However, over a longer time frame, this number seems aggressive. Several ship-tracking estimates are coming in much lower, ranging from 2m b/d to around 6m b/d.”
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

Title: India’s listless Hockey World Cup show sparks alarm

BENGALURU: If the eighth place in the FIH Pro League sounded the warning bells, the Indian men’s hockey team has done little to show they heard it.
On Friday, India will play Belgium in the 7-8 classification match of the World Cup. Monday’s 3-5 defeat to Argentina summed up a campaign littered with familiar flaws. There have been moments of promise in Amstelveen, but they have been overshadowed by defensive lapses, poor decision-making and an attack that has often failed to convert pressure into goals. Craig Fulton has fought to keep the players Hockey India was looking beyond; the South African got what he wanted to prepare the team, but does not have much to show in terms of results.
In five matches, India conceded 16 goals, while scoring 14, five of which were field goals. Off the 25 penalty corners earned, they converted seven, six of them by skipper
Harmanpreet Singh
.
Former India player and coach Jagbir Singh was scathing in his assessment of the team’s performance. He questioned the way India has approached the post-Olympic transition. “We have to stick to the Olympic cycle and prepare teams. After the Olympics is the period when you need to look ahead and prepare a team that can go from one Olympic year to the next and then maybe extend it based on their performance.
Which was not the case in this team. I don’t agree with a few selections, but it's all about the coach’s choice,” the 61-year-old explained. A “lack of consistency” was India’s biggest failing, said Jagbir.
For most of their campaign, the Indian defence crumbled under pressure. “Experienced players like Hardik were short of ideas, and the defenders looked clueless. Against Argentina are the trickiest team, we didn’t have players to take care of their players who were making all the difference,” pointed out the former India player. He was particularly critical of India’s midfield. “Which team can survive without a strong midfield in hockey? Where was India’s midfield?”
“We have a good midfield, but we didn’t even know what the transition of play was or how to attack from defence. Either we couldn't understand the coach's plan, or we couldn't adapt our strategy to the opponents,” he stated. The Indian team will have less than three weeks to pull their act together and head to Japan for the Asian Games, with an LA Olympics berth at stake for the defending champions.

Title: When Smaller Models Win

The following article originally appeared on the Asimov’s Addendum blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission.
Even the best AI models can suck at chess
The launch of ChatGPT had an interesting effect on the online chess discourse. Chess has already long been conquered by machines. As early as 1996 a computer (IBM’s Deep Blue) was able to beat the human world champion, grandmaster Garry Kasparov, in a game watched by over six million people.1 The world was shocked that a machine took on the best player and won a game, but chess engines didn’t stop evolving there. Since the ’90s, they have gotten better while the machines needed to run them have become much smaller. Today Stockfish is widely considered much stronger than any human player. It has run on consumer hardware since its launch in 2008, and by 2014 it was beating some of the world’s top grandmasters.
It came as a surprise to many, therefore, that modern LLMs, trained on a vast portion of the internet and requiring supercomputers to run, couldn’t help but cheat on almost every move. There are endless videos showing how just a few moves into a normal chess game, ChatGPT and some of its competitors would gladly throw the rules out the window to escape a checkmate or gain an advantage.
But in truth, this isn’t surprising. The LLMs were not trained with chess in mind. Sure, they may have seen countless chess games scattered throughout the internet, but the vast majority of their parameters and training compute were devoted to capabilities that are completely useless once you put a chessboard in front of them.2 Stockfish on the other hand uses a tree search algorithm that is built to be good at chess. If you want a chess engine, you use a chess engine.3
Smaller models are sometimes better
While chess is a particularly potent example of a large language model losing to a much smaller specialized system, it’s far from unique. In a 2025 position paper, NVIDIA researchers argued that small models4 (which it defines as models under 10 billion parameters) are the future of agentic AI and that they “provide significant benefits in cost-efficiency, adaptability, and deployment flexibility.”
Just because a larger model can do a job does not mean that a small model fine-tuned for that specific task can’t do it better and more cheaply. There are countless examples of smaller models doing just that. LiteResearcher is a 4B model that beat out Claude Sonnet 4.5 on some search benchmarks. Terminus-4B allows larger models to save compute by handing off terminal execution to a smaller model without suffering capability loss. The Docling family of open source models start at just 258 million parameters and allow for fast extraction of PDFs to text without having to feed 100-page PDFs into an expensive LLM. Researchers also trained a small 4B model to outperform even the GPT-5 series of models in a few social negotiation situations such as negotiating salary or bargaining for a purchase. Each wins, not by raw intelligence but because it is built or fine-tuned for a narrower, more specific purpose.
A frontier model may know how to do all of these jobs, but that doesn’t mean it’s the right tool for the job. Large models are expensive and unpredictable, and doubly so when it comes to agentic tasks which can span several turns and hundreds of thousands of tokens.
NVIDIA draws the line for small models at 10 billion parameters, but the more important boundary for developers may be whether a model is small enough to run yourself. There is still a whole class of models that are not necessarily small but are still small enough to fit on one consumer GPU (at least when quantized). This includes models like Qwen 3.8 27B, Gemma 4 26B and GPT-OSS 20B. These models are very capable even without specialization and rank very highly on benchmarks (with Qwen sometimes outranking top models from a few months ago). But they can still be easily run on premises without spending thousands of dollars on GPUs.
The ability to run smaller specialized models adds more than just efficiency; it provides a more realistic opportunity for a developer to train and fine-tune their own model, and to host the model locally or in the cloud instead of relying on the model provider to do so for it. This in turn can provide developers more control over how tokens are used, how outputs are structured, and how each part of the pipeline can be improved individually—instead of assuming an improvement in the most popular benchmarks will lead to every task improving. And as noted above, smaller models can be easier to fine-tune, thereby creating a more specialized AI. As my colleague Ilan Strauss has noted, specialization is a powerful economic force.
How do you train it, and where does it run?
The strongest argument for using an off-the-shelf generic chat model is often one of convenience. For most tasks a general model will be good enough, and with products like OpenRouter, developers can easily pick and choose from hundreds of models (plenty of them open source) all competing in capability and cost without putting in any upfront work to train a model. As Raffi Krikorian of Mozilla noted while reviewing this article, generic models also make particular sense early in a company’s lifecycle, when the problem itself is still being defined. At that stage, experimenting with the largest and most capable model available can help a team figure out exactly what it needs. But as the problem space narrows and the required architecture becomes clearer, so too may the need for a large generic model. And despite many first-party model makers discontinuing their fine-tuning products, fine-tuning and hosting a smaller model remains relatively easy, largely thanks to parameter-efficient techniques like LoRA.
LoRA
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) allows developers to fine-tune a model without touching the actual model weights. It works by attaching a relatively small number of trainable weights that are updated during fine-tuning. This is important for several reasons. A small adapter can be easily transported, and serving a new LoRA does not require loading an entirely new model as long as the underlying base model is already available. Unlike full fine-tuning, a LoRA also reduces the risk of catastrophic forgetting.
Training a LoRA is much cheaper than full fine-tuning as it only updates a small selection of weights. This can be done on consumer GPUs using libraries such as Hugging Face Transformers or Unsloth. There are also APIs that mimic or improve on the fine-tuning APIs that used to be provided by the big three providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google), Fireworks, for example, provides a straightforward fine-tuning API that takes example completions for it to learn from. Going beyond SFT (supervised fine-tuning, or learning by example), Tinker allows developers to build custom RL (reinforcement learning) environments that reward results meeting certain criteria, while the environment itself runs on the developer’s machine.
Hosting a LoRA is similarly straightforward and, importantly, portable across platforms. Transferring a fully fine-tuned model to a new API platform can be costly and may require the provider to serve your model separately on expensive GPUs. Using LoRA allows the platform to just load a small adapter onto the model they are already using to serve other users’ requests. This means that fine-tuning a LoRA does not lock you to a specific platform, and it also doesn’t force you to rent your own GPUs.
Control beyond the model weights
As Tim O’Reilly previously argued, open source AI should not stop at the model weights. In a similar vein, the possibilities for developers building a custom system do not stop there either. Model APIs are inherently limiting, they impose on you what parts of the model’s input can be touched, what can be cached, and how you can affect the output. Going back to the chess example, enforcing valid chess moves at output time is easy, assuming you have access to the code that runs the model, but it’s not easy to do when you are relying on an API built for a chatbot that you are unable to modify.
Self-hosting a model gives you a level of control far beyond what is possible through a standard chat completion API and allows you to build the model around the task instead of building the task around the model. Fine-tuning is only one aspect of specialization. You can also constrain which outputs are valid, expose and modify probabilities of every token, cache any state, and add task-specific logic directly into the inference pipeline.
This matters because the default approach to improving AI systems has increasingly become to reach for a more capable general model. Sometimes that is the right answer. But improving general model intelligence is only one lever, and often not the cheapest or most reliable one.
In 1997 nobody complained that Deep Blue gave bad recipes because it wasn’t built to do anything but play chess. By specializing around one narrow problem, it was able to beat a grandmaster at a game that many had thought machines would never conquer.
The lesson from LLMs cheating at chess is that the best tool for a problem is often not the most general one. Super general intelligence does not automatically translate into high capabilities in specialized tasks. The opposite is closer to being true. Specialized machine intelligence requires lots of data and often its own pipeline. Small models can help companies get there.5

Title: Sevan missing Konaseema fishermen found safe off West Bengal coast

The seven fishermen from Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema district in Andhra Pradesh, who went missing in the sea on August 7, were found safe near Shankarpur fishing harbour off West Bengal coast on Wednesday.
Contact with the fishermen was lost on August 7 after they went deep-sea fishing off the Andhra coast in search of tuna. They set sail into the sea on a mechanised boat from Odalrevu fish landing point.
On Wednesday afternoon, local fishermen found the boat with the missing fishermen on board near the Shankarpur fishing harbour.
Later, they gave a cellphone to the missing fishermen, who spoke to their family members in Andhra Pradesh, confirming that they were safe. The fishermen said that they were stranded at sea after the boat engine developed a technical snag.
The fishermen on board the missing boat have been identified as Kopanathi Ramakrishna, 49, of Komarigiri village; Kollati Yesudasu, 49, of Bendamuri Lanka; Palepu Santa Rao, 26, and Kollati Srinubabu, 37, of Odalarevu village; Karri Rambabu, 46, of Komarigiripatnam in Allavaram mandal. The remaining fishermen are Sangani Tatarao, 60, of Katrenikona mandal and Kataadi Satish Kumar of I. Polavaram mandal.
Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema District Collector R. Mahesh Kumar was alerted by the families of the missing fishermen.
Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed the Collector to initiate measures for the safe return of the fishermen to their homes. He thanked the Indian Navy, Coast Guard and Central Marine agencies for extending timely support for the two-week search operation in the sea.
A team of Fisheries Department officials have left for West Bengal to bring the missing fishermen back home, the Collector said.
“The family members of the missing fishermen alerted the district administration that the missing fishermen had been traced to West Bengal. The boat drifted towards the West Bengal coast after the engine developed a technical glitch,” District Joint Director (Fisheries) K. Karunakar told The Hindu.
In an official release, Agriculture Minister and Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema District In-charge Minister K. Atchannaidu said, “We have confirmed the presence of the missing fishermen who were facilitated to speak to their families.”
Indian Navy and Coast Guard had been deployed for the search operation since August 17. Mr. Atchannaidu thanked the Eastern Naval Command of the Indian Navy and Coast Guard for their timely response.
‘Survived without food for three days’
The fishermen said that they survived without food for more than three days in the sea before they reached the West Bengal coast.
In a telephonic conversation with his family members on Wednesday, Karri Rambabu, 47, shared their ordeals. “We ran out of food stock three days ago. Before it, we managed with the available food stocks, with regular intervals of fasting. We survived without food for three days. The locals of Shankarpur fishing harbour found us at around 11.30 a.m. on Wednesday, Mr. Rambabu, hailing from Komaragiripatnam village said.

Title: One migrant raid in New Jersey, 46 lives destroyed: ‘My life is incomplete without my daughter’

María Eugenia García’s second daughter was born prematurely. Killy Tatiana Yangquen García arrived at seven months, tiny and fragile, entirely dependent on her mother’s protection. She spent her first 20 years clinging to María Eugenia, the two never far from each other. Until Killy Tatiana was arrested in an immigration raid at the bonded warehouse where she was working without papers on a cursed October morning. “Do you understand the care I’ve taken with her and that they ripped her away from me like that? And me not being able to protect her? I haven’t seen her since, only by video call,” the mother sobs from her home in the New Jersey city of Elizabeth, where she has been hiding since her daughter was detained and sent back to Colombia, the country they left more than a decade ago.
Sitting at her kitchen table under the protection of the air conditioning on a hot June afternoon, between sobs and pounding the table when anguish overwhelms her, 53-year-old María Eugenia recounts what EL PAÍS was able to reconstruct over three months and a dozen interviews: how a raid shattered the lives of roughly 50 people and their families.
It was early morning on October 29, 2025. Killy Tatiana was supposed to work remotely, but she was asked to go into the office. María Eugenia was the first to leave the house. She went, as usual, to help care for her sister’s baby. “I arrived, put the little girl to bed and fell asleep too. I didn’t know what was happening behind the door. I slept for an hour, but it was a deep sleep; I don’t understand how that day I was so sleepy,” the mother says.
When she woke up, the first thing she saw was the anguished face of her older daughter. “She says to me: ‘Mom, sit down, do you want herbal tea, water? I don’t have good news. There was a raid at Savino. Immigration came and took Tatiana,’” María Eugenia recalls, vividly remembering one of the worst moments of her life.
That day, immigration agents stormed the Savino del Bene warehouse, an Italian international shipping company that moves fashion and luxury goods. The facility is located in the Avenel area of Woodbridge, New Jersey, less than an hour’s drive from Manhattan. Witnesses who spoke to this newspaper said more than 50 agents from multiple Department of Homeland Security agencies arrived: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), among others.
“The operation was large. They came with long guns — the military, the police, and ICE — and surrounded the place. Even a helicopter. They climbed onto the roofs. They wouldn’t let anyone leave. They arrived with wall-scanning devices and with dogs that went through every area, searching for people,” recalls Sandra Suero, whose son, 18-year-old Jhonatan Bello Cabrera, was inside the warehouse during the raid. The Colombian youth managed to call his mother while hiding from agents, and she arrived at the site immediately.
In total, 46 people were arrested — a quarter of the employees present that day — in the operation. According to the pro-immigrant group Movimiento Cosecha, which has advised the families, at least 30 of the workers had pending asylum applications, and many had work permits. That matters little in the Trump era: “An employment authorization card, by itself, does not confer legal status in the United States. Likewise, a pending asylum application, by itself, does not confer legal immigration status on a foreign national,” a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told this newspaper.
“They asked me if I had a work permit. I showed it to them. I told them I was in the process of getting residency and they checked it on a computer and took the permit away. They asked where my personal things were and then they handcuffed me and took me out,” Jhonatan says.
When he was detained, Jhonatan was in the middle of a family petition process to obtain permanent residency through his mother’s husband. His stepfather was a naturalized U.S. citizen and his mother a legal permanent resident. The Colombian national, who had been in the United States for five years at the time, was processed and sent first to an ICE facility in the state, then to Texas, and eventually to Arizona. In total, he spent two months detained until he was released in December after posting a $6,000 bond and being fitted with an ankle monitor.
“You’re supposed to be safe at work. They weren’t committing crimes or anything close to it. Why do they go and take working people away? According to the government, according to the laws, they were supposed to start removing criminal elements, but they didn’t do that,” says his mother, Sandra. “We never thought something like this would happen, especially to a newly graduated kid, still a child, because he’s just starting his life. He had just turned 18 and they arrested him,” she laments. The next hearing in her son’s case is scheduled for November of next year. Jhonatan is trying not to think about what could happen in the months ahead.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 promising to carry out “the largest deportation in history,” his administration has employed all the tools in its arsenal to pursue, arrest, and expel as many migrants as possible. With daily arrest quotas, massive and indiscriminate raids and canceled humanitarian protections, the Republican administration has launched an unprecedented anti-immigrant crackdown.
Trump’s so-called border czar, Tom Homan, even predicted in May of that year that the country would see more ICE workplace operations than in any previous period of U.S. history. Homan described the strategy as “flooding the area,” for its depth and speed. That’s how dozens of migrants were detained at processing plants and construction sites.
Another front of that offensive has been bonded warehouses like Savino del Bene. Facilities like this were little known until the Trump administration decided to use them in its campaign against immigration. They are places where companies store goods pending payment of import taxes. In return, they are overseen by customs officials who can enter to inspect products when they wish.
Northern New Jersey is full of bonded warehouses because of its proximity to one of the United States’ main seaports. Since last year, federal agents have conducted raids at at least five such facilities in the state. In total, more than 200 people have been detained, local activists say.
“A kind of legal fiction”
Advocates for migrant workers in these warehouses have repeatedly questioned the legality of the arrests. For Lauren Wilfong of the National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON), there is no doubt these arrests “violate the U.S. Constitution, federal civil rights law, and the human rights of members of our community.”
In March, NDLON, along with other pro-immigrant organizations in New Jersey, filed a request under the Freedom of Information Act with the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, and CBP seeking records on these raids to prove their illegality. The government never responded, so the organization filed a lawsuit on August 11 to force it to release the documents.
“These bonded warehouses work just like any other warehouse, but there’s this sort of legal fiction that exists,” Wilfong explains by phone. “Because they hold goods that have not been processed yet for importing, it does give the Customs and Border Protection Agency certain rights as far as inspecting the products and things like that. But these are rights regarding the goods that are held there, not the workers at those facilities,” she says. “In a site like that, the Constitution actually requires that law enforcement have a warrant in order to demand entry, and they don’t have warrants.”
The Department of Homeland Security maintains it does not need a warrant to carry out these inspections and operations. “A bonded warehouse is within CBP search authority and a search may be conducted at any time, without a warrant, to include both people and things,” it said in a statement.
Asked by EL PAÍS whether the company responsible for the warehouse, Savino del Bene, faced penalties for employing undocumented people, a department spokesperson responded in general terms, saying that “as part of compliance reviews, CBP validates the employee lists provided” by each bonded warehouse. Any noncompliance results in “immediate corrective action requirements” and can lead to “loss of warehouse designation, and referral to the authorities.” It was unclear whether Savino del Bene faced any such consequences. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
As this becomes one of the many legal battles the Trump administration faces over its immigration policy, Wilfong stresses that “the scale of the harm” in this case “goes well beyond the people arrested” in the raids and affects “everyone in those warehouses and then, of course, all their families as well.”
María Eugenia García last saw her daughter Killy Tatiana at a detention center in New Jersey before she was moved around the country and sent to Colombia. “My life is incomplete without her,” the mother laments. Separated from her daughter for the first time, she says she has had to learn to dry her tears, “breathe, go on, and endure.” But for how long? she asks. “I have had a lot of strength from God. It’s the only thing that has given me the courage not to die before seeing her. Because I couldn’t have done it alone,” she says.
Hope of voluntary departure
Killy Tatiana answers the video call from Bogotá, where she has lived since leaving the United States in February with a voluntary departure granted by an immigration judge after nearly four months in detention. “When they grabbed me, it was hard for me because I said, ‘My God!’ It was something we were aware could happen. I had thought several times about quitting my job, but I never said anything. So if I had quit, I wouldn’t have been there,” she says.
Killy Tatiana came to the U.S. with her family when she was 10. She turned 21 last May and celebrated — if that word can be used — by video call with her family in New Jersey. In Bogotá, some relatives took her in, but for her, Colombia is a country she doesn’t know anymore, no longer hers after so much time away. “I stay locked up. I get bored because my life, my social circle, is my mom, my sister, my niece and my husband. It’s a big shock for me to leave them and be here locked up with no one,” she says, trying to hold back tears.
Her mother and husband are aware of the blow returning to Colombia has proven to be, and they suffer along with her. “It’s hard because you’re sending someone [away] whose whole life is here. I understand that there are laws. The law must be respected, but we were also making an effort to legalize her. It’s inexplicable. Because you feel empty, helpless knowing nothing can be done,” says Yardanis Payero, her husband of two years, who lives with María Eugenia in New Jersey.
María Eugenia’s family entered the country on visas and, like so many immigrant families, stayed after their permissions expired. They were undocumented for 10 years, until Killy Tatiana was detained. “We thought we didn’t need papers because back then you could live without papers. We never rushed it,” she explains.
However, mother and daughter acknowledge they began to realize they would need to regularize their status in some way when Trump secured his return to power in 2024. “Once detentions started, we knew we were at risk. We knew both she and I were vulnerable to being picked up at any moment. We always thought about what we would do if it happened. And we would say: ‘If they pick me up, I’ll sign and leave immediately,’” María Eugenia says.
That was the plan, and it played out to the letter. But it was heartbreaking. It’s easier to speak hypothetically than to live through it. María Eugenia came to believe that because Killy Tatiana had spent half her life in the United States and had no criminal record, there was a possibility she could stay in the country after her arrest: “We had our hopes, but the judge denied bond. And they told her she would be deported, and with that there was no chance of returning. So they told her it was better to sign the voluntary departure.”
Under U.S. law, a voluntary departure is a mechanism that allows a person to avoid an order of deportation by agreeing to leave the country on their own. It is useful for those who have a legal route to return to the U.S., such as a family reunification petition, because it removes the usual five- to 10-year bar on reentry associated with deportations.
In Killy Tatiana’s case, her hope is that her husband, who is applying for citizenship, will be able to bring her back once that process is complete. However, that could take years.
“Here are the bitches”
In the months that the Savino del Bene warehouse workers were held in detention, their relatives and loved ones in New Jersey never stopped fighting for their release, even after authorities transferred them to facilities in Texas, Ohio and Michigan. A group of 10 women detained together in the October raid were sent to Michigan — a state on the Canadian border. There, at the North Lake Correctional Facility, almost four hours from Michigan’s main airport and in the middle of a forest, the women endured the worst months of the Upper Midwest’s freezing winter.
They arrived in Michigan after first passing through the infamous ICE facility in Newark, on the outskirts of New York, called Delaney Hall, where hundreds of detainees have protested the awful conditions: rotten food and restricted visits. The transfer from New Jersey was days of hell, during which they were offered little food or water, the women told this newspaper. They were first taken to the “iceboxes” of Texas, as the southern border detention facilities are known for their freezing temperatures. From there, they went to Ohio and spent a few days in a county jail. Upon arrival, they all recall being forced to undress in front of a female officer and shower while she watched. When they finally reached the Michigan facility, they had suffered taunts and humiliations that were hard to forget.
“When the immigration officer was handing us over to the county sheriff in Ohio, he said: ‘Here are the bitches,’” recalls Sofía, one of the detained women. “In Michigan they didn’t turn on the heat. Every day we had nosebleeds from the cold. We slept together until we warmed up. We stuffed sanitary pads into the vents. The food was bad. You’d find pieces of bone, teeth, bread with mold. Horrible,” says another detainee.
To cope, the women forged a friendship that has endured long after their release. For the last of them to regain her freedom, an Ecuadorian immigrant who was ultimately deported, detention lasted seven months.
Sofía, a 27-year-old Dominican woman who prefers to keep her real name private, is remembered as the person who made everyone laugh, who looked for “the bright side” even in the darkest moments of her detention. She was deported to the Dominican Republic on January 27 of this year, 91 days after she was arrested at the warehouse, where she had been working without papers. Although she had overstayed the visa she used to enter five years earlier and was undocumented, she never thought she could be picked up while working. Her mother, however, had a premonition.
On the day of the raid, her 51-year-old mother was traveling from Puerto Rico, where she lives, to New Jersey to surprise her with a visit. “But before I arrived, I was surprised to find out that my daughter had already been arrested. Although I had told her on several occasions to stop working, she has always been very independent. She likes to be on her own,” says her mother, still in disbelief — and who also asks that her identity be protected — during a joint video call with EL PAÍS.
Both are now separated by the Mona Channel, the stretch of water between the Dominican Republic and Puerto Rico, with no idea when they might see each other again. Sofía cannot enter Puerto Rico because it is a U.S. territory and, after being deported, she is barred from returning to the United States for several years. Her mother, though a permanent resident with the right to travel, doesn’t have enough money to do so often and has been able to visit only once.
“Being close and far away has its pros and cons. It’s as if you had someone right next to you whom you want to visit, but you can’t whenever you want,” laments the mother, though she hasn’t lost hope that somehow she’ll be able to get her daughter out of the country they emigrated from due to a lack of economic opportunities. Sofía, for her part, maintains that she doesn’t want to return to the United States permanently: “I feel — I don’t know if it’s shame — about going back to that country after what they did to me.”
Free but terrified
On a living-room wall at Daniela’s house hangs a kind of altar that reminds her of the time she spent detained. Or rather, what kept her sane during the more than two months she was locked up after the Avenel raid: faith. During the weeks the group of women spent in Michigan, Daniela (an assumed name) found God. She was baptized inside the detention center and still proudly shows her baptism certificate.
To get through the days, Daniela studied the Bible. She began copying verses and prayers onto colored poster board whenever the detention center guards were kind enough to lend her a pencil sharpener. She wrote letters to her two children that she never mailed but kept in a book. Today, in her basement apartment in Elizabeth, some of those writings cover one wall of her living room.
Daniela, 45, came to New Jersey 10 years ago. She took her two children and fled Colombia, where she had been threatened with death. In the United States, she sought asylum and received a Social Security number and work authorization. “That’s when I started working. I started doing taxes. I always did everything right. From the start my lawyer told me: ‘Never ask for help here in the country, never.’ And that’s what I did. I never asked for anything here. I always worked; I learned to do everything — lay floors, construction pads, paint, everything. I raised my children,” she says.
They waited years for their asylum appointment. Finally, they got a slot last August. Daniela went with her children and her lawyer for the interview. In the middle of it, the official “stood up, left, and ICE arrived.” “Six agents came in. They pushed my son against the wall, put chains on him and took him away,” she recalls, still shocked.
Her eldest son, 24 and married to a U.S. citizen, spent 100 days in detention. During that time, Daniela was also picked up in the warehouse raid. Her younger son, 19, was left alone; he had to drop out of school and start working to support himself.
“It was very hard, but I say God has a purpose because we both came out free. It’s a blessing,” the mother says. When her son was released from detention, she was still being held. By the time her turn finally came, after posting a $10,000 bond, her son drove 27 hours to pick her up in Michigan on January 10. They had spent the first Christmas of their lives apart.
Back home, however, the torment has not ended. “When I got out, I shut myself in for a month. I gained 29 pounds from anxiety. I kept the windows closed; I didn’t even go to the door. I kept watch, afraid they might knock. It was a horrible unease,” Daniela explains. “Reintegrating into society is hard. It has been very difficult for me.” It hasn’t helped that people have continued to be arrested in her neighborhood. The day before meeting EL PAÍS at her home, she says a migrant was detained around the corner.
She knows little about the status of her asylum petition. She says she was given several court dates that were canceled: “When I check the app, it says this case is pending.” “About two months ago I got a call from an asylum office telling me I had to go with an ID to pick up a paper. And I said: ‘No, my dear, I’m not going.’” She knows the risk of leaving her house perfectly well, so she prefers to leave it in God’s hands.
